title: Evaporation and condensation: why some liquids leave fast, where the heat goes, and what salt does to the air

summary.text: A drop of hand sanitiser vanishes from your hand in seconds and leaves it cold. A drop of water takes minutes, and a drop of coconut oil never leaves at all. All three sit in the same air. In the monsoon, a spoon of salt left on a shelf turns damp, though nothing cold has touched it. In this unit your child races six liquids across a steel plate, boils water with the lid on and with the lid off, and finds which kitchen things pull water out of the air. Then they find out where the heat goes. Evaporation takes heat from what is left. Condensation gives it back, in a fridge, an air conditioner and a monsoon cloud.
summary.art: A steel plate with six wet streaks in a ring, some already dry, with a hand beside it holding a drop of sanitiser, and a small dish of damp salt beside a closed jar of dry salt.

intro.hook: Put one drop of water and one drop of hand sanitiser on the back of your hand. The sanitiser is gone in seconds, and your skin feels much colder where it was. The water takes minutes and feels only a little cool. Both are at room warmth. So why do they leave at such different speeds, and where does the cold come from?
intro.text: Water is always leaving wet things as vapour and coming back as drops. A damp cloth dries only when more water leaves it than comes back. In this unit you ask harder questions. Which liquids leave fastest, and why? Where does the heat go when a liquid leaves, and where does it go when the vapour turns back into drops? And why does a spoon of salt turn damp in a monsoon room when nothing cold has touched it? You answer these questions with a steel plate, two pans and a humid box.
intro.art: A child holding two hands out, a droplet of clear liquid on the back of each, with tiny wavy arrows rising from one drop quickly and from the other slowly.

outcomes: I can explain that different liquids evaporate at different speeds, and that how fast a liquid leaves depends on how tightly its own particles hold each other.
I can explain that evaporation takes heat from the liquid that is left behind, and that condensation gives heat out.
I can use this to explain how a fridge or an air conditioner moves heat from inside to outside.
I can explain why a pan with a lid loses almost no water while a pan without a lid loses a lot, and why boiling water in a lid-on pan does not boil hotter.
I can explain that air can carry only a certain amount of water vapour, that the amount grows quickly as air gets warmer, and what relative humidity and dew point mean.
I can show that some things, such as salt, pull water out of the air even when they are not cold, and say why this makes a salt box go damp in the monsoon.
I can say that a solid, such as camphor, can turn straight into a gas, and name one place where this happens at home.
I can tell how William Cullen showed that cold can be made by a liquid evaporating, with no cold thing added.

terms.meaning: Liquid turning into gas at its surface. The fastest particles leave first.
terms.example: A wet streak on a steel plate dries because its water evaporates.
terms.art: A wet streak on a plate with wavy arrows rising from it.

terms.meaning: Gas turning back into liquid, often when it touches something cooler.
terms.example: Drops form on the underside of a pot lid when the vapour from the dal meets the cooler lid.
terms.art: A pot lid with drops under it, and arrows of vapour rising to meet it.

terms.meaning: Water as an invisible gas, mixed in the air.
terms.example: The air in your room carries water vapour even when it feels dry.
terms.art: A clear room drawn with a few tiny dots floating in the air.

terms.meaning: A liquid is volatile if it evaporates easily and fast at normal room warmth.
terms.example: Alcohol in hand sanitiser is volatile. Coconut oil is not.
terms.art: Two drops on a plate, one with many arrows rising and one with almost none.

terms.meaning: How full of water vapour the air is, compared with the most it can carry at its temperature. It is written as a percentage.
terms.example: Air at 70 per cent humidity carries seven tenths of the most vapour it can carry at that temperature.
terms.art: A cup drawn as a tall glass filled to the 70 per cent mark with blue dots.

terms.meaning: Air that carries all the water vapour it can at its temperature. Its relative humidity is 100 per cent.
terms.example: Fog forms when air near the ground becomes saturated.
terms.art: A glass drawn completely full of blue dots with a line marked 100 per cent.

terms.meaning: The temperature to which air must be cooled for it to become saturated. Anything colder than this gets drops of water on it.
terms.example: If the dew point is 24 degrees, a steel glass at 20 degrees gets mist and a glass at 28 degrees stays dry.
terms.art: A thermometer with a mark at 24 degrees and two glasses, a cold one misted and a warm one dry.

terms.meaning: The temperature at which a liquid boils. For water it is 100 degrees Celsius at sea level and lower on a hill.
terms.example: Water boils at about 92 degrees at Ooty, which is about 2,200 metres high.
terms.art: A pan of bubbling water with a thermometer reading 100 beside a hill with a thermometer reading 92.

terms.meaning: How hard a gas or liquid pushes on each bit of a surface. The air pushes on everything around you.
terms.example: A pressure cooker raises the pressure on the water, so the water boils at a higher temperature.
terms.art: A pressure cooker with arrows pushing on the lid from inside and a thin arrow of air outside.

terms.meaning: The heat that goes into turning a liquid into a gas, or comes out when a gas turns back into a liquid. It does not change the temperature.
terms.example: Boiling away 1 kilogram of water takes more than five times as much heat as warming it from freezing to boiling.
terms.art: A pan on a stove with a thermometer stuck at 100 degrees while a large flame arrow goes into the water.

terms.meaning: The special liquid inside a fridge or air conditioner that evaporates to take heat in and condenses to give heat out.
terms.example: In a fridge, the refrigerant evaporates in pipes inside the cold box and condenses in pipes at the back.
terms.art: A loop of pipe with a cold part labelled evaporates and a warm part labelled condenses.

terms.meaning: Able to pull water vapour out of the air. Salt, sugar and jaggery are hygroscopic.
terms.example: Table salt gets damp on a rainy day, because it pulls water from the air.
terms.art: A small dish of salt with tiny drops forming on the grains and dots arriving from the air.

terms.meaning: A solid turning directly into a gas, without becoming a liquid first.
terms.example: A camphor tablet slowly shrinks in the open without leaving any liquid.
terms.art: A camphor tablet with a smell shown as wavy lines rising and no puddle beneath.

terms.meaning: Ice that forms directly from water vapour, on a surface colder than zero degrees.
terms.example: White frost on the walls of a freezer is made from water vapour in the air.
terms.art: The inside of a freezer with white feathery frost on the wall and arrows from the air.

terms.meaning: The lowest temperature you could reach by cooling something with water evaporating from it. It combines heat and humidity in one number.
terms.example: A hot day with high humidity has a high wet-bulb temperature, and sweat cools you less.
terms.art: A thermometer with a wet cloth around its bulb in a breeze, reading lower than a dry thermometer beside it.

terms.meaning: The flat lower edge of a cloud, where rising air has cooled to its dew point.
terms.example: On a hot afternoon, fair-weather clouds have flat bottoms at the same height.
terms.art: A row of white clouds with flat dark bottoms along the same level over a green field.

explanations.concept: Different liquids leave at different speeds
explanations.definition: A liquid is volatile if its particles hold each other weakly, so many escape each second. A liquid whose particles hold each other tightly evaporates slowly.
explanations.description: In every liquid, particles are moving and bumping, and some at the surface are fast enough to break free. How many break free each second depends on how tightly the others are holding them. Alcohol molecules hold each other weakly, so many escape each second. That is why hand sanitiser dries in seconds. Water molecules hold each other more tightly, so water dries slowly. The molecules of coconut oil are long and tangled, and they cling to each other so tightly that hardly any escape at room warmth. Salt and sugar dissolved in water make it dry a little more slowly, because the dissolved particles get in the way and stay behind. The boiling points of these liquids show the same order. Alcohol boils at about 78 degrees, water at 100 and oils at far higher temperatures.
examples: Hand sanitiser dries in seconds, water in minutes, and coconut oil stays for days.
Nail polish remover and petrol are volatile, which is why their smell spreads so fast.
Sugar syrup dries slowly and leaves a sticky film, because the sugar stays behind.
explanations.art: Three zoomed-in liquid surfaces side by side: alcohol with many particles escaping, water with a few and oil with almost none.
explanations.context: This card explains why the six liquids in the Drop Race leave at different speeds.

explanations.concept: Evaporation takes heat from what is left
explanations.definition: When a liquid evaporates, the fastest and most energetic particles are the ones that escape. The liquid left behind has lost energy, so it gets cooler.
explanations.description: Heat is the movement energy of particles. The particles that escape from a liquid are the fastest ones. When they leave, they take their energy with them, and the average energy of the particles left behind falls. The liquid cools, and so does whatever it touches. This is why sweat cools your skin, why hand sanitiser feels colder than water, and why a wet cloth feels cool in a breeze. The faster a liquid evaporates, the faster it takes heat away. Nothing cold has to arrive. Something warm has to leave.
examples: Sanitiser feels colder on your hand than water because it evaporates faster.
Coming out of a bath, you feel cold until you are dry.
A clay pot of water stays cool because water seeps through the clay and evaporates from the outside.
explanations.art: A hand with a drop of sanitiser on it, fast particles flying off the drop carrying red heat arrows away, and the skin below shown turning blue.
explanations.context: In the Drop Race, the drop of sanitiser on your hand felt colder than the drop of water. This card explains why.

explanations.definition: When water vapour turns back into liquid, it gives out the same heat it took in when it evaporated. This is why condensation warms the thing it forms on.
explanations.description: Every gram of water that evaporates takes a lot of heat with it. When that vapour turns back into drops, the same heat comes out again. This is why steam at 100 degrees can burn you worse than boiling water at 100 degrees. The steam gives up all its latent heat as it condenses on your skin, on top of the heat it gives out as it cools. The same thing warms the air when a monsoon cloud forms. The Sun's heat evaporated sea water, and the vapour carried that heat up. When the vapour turns to cloud drops high above, the heat is released into the air around, and that warm air rises further. Tropical storms and thunderclouds get much of their power this way.
examples: Steam from a kettle burns more than boiling water, because condensing steam gives out its latent heat.
Warm, moist air rising in a monsoon cloud gets extra warmth as its vapour condenses into drops.
The cool glass of a window gets slightly warmer as drops form on it.
explanations.art: A sea surface with heat arrows going up in vapour, a cloud forming above with heat arrows going out of it, and warm air rising from the cloud.
explanations.context: This card explains where the heat goes when vapour turns back into drops.

explanations.concept: How a fridge and an air conditioner move heat
explanations.definition: A fridge and an air conditioner use a liquid that evaporates inside, taking heat in, and condenses outside, giving heat out. They move heat from a cold place to a warmer place.
explanations.description: Inside a fridge, a pipe carries a special liquid called a refrigerant. In the pipes inside the cold box, the refrigerant evaporates and takes heat from the food and the air. A pump called a compressor squeezes the vapour, which makes it hot. The hot vapour flows through the pipes at the back of the fridge, where it condenses and gives out heat to the kitchen. That is why the back of a fridge is warm. The liquid then flows back inside, and the loop starts again. An air conditioner works the same way. The room unit is the cold part, and the box outside is the warm part. Heat does not flow from a cold place to a warm place by itself, so the compressor needs electricity to push it that way.
examples: The back and sides of a running fridge are warm.
The outdoor box of an air conditioner blows out warm air.
A fridge left with its door open warms the kitchen. It gives out heat at the back, and the cold inside cannot cool the whole room.
explanations.art: A fridge with a pipe loop: a cold pipe inside labelled evaporates and a warm pipe at the back labelled condenses, with heat arrows going out.
explanations.context: This card explains how a fridge cools its inside by warming the room, which you feel in the Feel the Heat Leave activity.

explanations.concept: Air can carry only so much water vapour, and warm air carries much more
explanations.definition: At each temperature there is a limit to how much water vapour air can carry, and the limit rises quickly as the air gets warmer. At 20 degrees Celsius it is about 17 grams in every cubic metre, and at 30 degrees it is about 30 grams.
explanations.description: Air does not soak up water like a sponge. Water vapour mixes in among the air particles, and how much can stay as vapour depends on the temperature. At 10 degrees, a cubic metre of air can carry about 9 grams of water vapour. At 20 degrees it is about 17 grams, at 30 degrees about 30 grams, and at 40 degrees about 51 grams. So air at 30 degrees can carry about 3 times as much water vapour as air at 10 degrees. If the air carries all it can, it is saturated. If you cool saturated air a little, some of its vapour has to condense into drops. This is why warm, damp tropical air makes such heavy rain when it rises and cools.
examples: A cubic metre of air at 30 degrees can carry about 30 grams of water vapour, which is more than a small spoonful.
A room 4 metres by 3 metres by 3 metres can hold more than a litre of water as vapour when saturated at 30 degrees.
Cold winter air can carry little vapour, which is why it feels dry even when it is foggy.
explanations.art: A bar chart of grams of water vapour a cubic metre of air can carry at 10, 20, 30 and 40 degrees, with the bars growing taller.
explanations.context: This card gives the numbers behind the idea that warm air carries more water vapour.

explanations.definition: Relative humidity tells you how full the air is, as a percentage of the most it can carry. The dew point is the temperature to which the air must be cooled to become completely full.
explanations.description: A weather report may say 70 per cent humidity at 30 degrees. That means the air holds 70 per cent of the most it could hold at 30 degrees, about 21 grams in each cubic metre. If this air is cooled, the same 21 grams stay in each cubic metre, but the most the air can carry falls. At about 24 degrees, the most it can carry has fallen to 21 grams, and the air is full. That temperature, 24 degrees, is the dew point. Any surface colder than the dew point gets drops. A dew point close to the air temperature means very damp air. The dew point is a better sign than humidity of how muggy it feels, because it does not change when the air warms or cools.
examples: A steel glass at 20 degrees mists in a room where the dew point is 24 degrees.
In the Chennai monsoon the dew point can be above 25 degrees, so a glass of tap water can mist.
Fog forms when the air near the ground cools to its dew point.
explanations.art: A thermometer showing 30 degrees air temperature and a second mark at 24 degrees dew point, with a cold glass below the dew point misted.
explanations.context: This card explains relative humidity and dew point, which you use in the Will It Mist? game.

explanations.concept: Boiling, pressure and the pressure cooker
explanations.definition: A liquid boils when its vapour can push back the air and form bubbles inside the liquid. Higher air pressure raises the boiling point, and lower air pressure lowers it.
explanations.description: Boiling is not only very fast evaporation. When water is hot enough, vapour forms inside the liquid as bubbles, and the bubbles can only grow if the vapour pushes harder than the air pressing on the water. High on a hill the air presses less, so water boils at a lower temperature, about one degree lower for every 300 metres you climb. On Mount Everest, water boils at only about 70 degrees. In a pressure cooker the lid holds the steam in and the pressure rises, so the water boils at about 120 degrees. The hotter water cooks food faster. In an open pan, the water cannot get hotter than its boiling point, however big the flame. A bigger flame only makes it boil away faster.
examples: Rice takes longer to cook at Ooty than in Chennai, because the water boils at a lower temperature.
A pressure cooker cooks dal faster because its water gets hotter than 100 degrees.
A big flame under an open pan of boiling water does not make the water any hotter. It boils away faster.
explanations.art: Three pans on a mountain slope, at sea level, at Ooty and on Everest, each with a thermometer reading 100, 92 and 70.
explanations.context: This card explains why a lid-on pan does not boil hotter, and why a pressure cooker does.

explanations.concept: Why a lid keeps the water in the pan
explanations.definition: A lid stops vapour escaping. The vapour hits the cooler lid, condenses and drips back into the pan, and the lid also keeps the heat in.
explanations.description: In an open pan of boiling water, the vapour rises and drifts into the kitchen, so the water level falls. Under a lid, the vapour hits the underside of the lid, which is cooler than the vapour. It condenses into drops, which run down and fall back into the pan. The water leaves and comes back, so the level hardly changes. The lid also keeps in the heat that the vapour carries, because the condensing drops give out their latent heat to the lid and the pan. That is why a covered pan comes to the boil sooner and uses less fuel. The water in a covered pan still boils at 100 degrees. The lid saves heat and water, but it does not raise the boiling point.
examples: Cooks cover a pan of rice so that the steam stays in and the pan comes to the boil faster.
Water dripping off the lid of an idli steamer is steam that has condensed.
Dal cooked in an open pan boils down to a thicker mixture, and under a lid it does not.
explanations.art: Two pans, one open with vapour drifting away and the water level low, and one with a lid and drops running down the lid back into the pan.
explanations.context: This card explains the result of the Lid On or Lid Off experiment.

explanations.concept: Thirsty things: how salt pulls water from the air
explanations.definition: A hygroscopic substance pulls water vapour from the air without being cold. Salt does this when the humidity is above about 75 per cent.
explanations.description: Water vapour does not need a cold surface to turn into a liquid. It also turns into a liquid on things that hold on to water very strongly. A grain of salt holds water so well that, when the air is more than about 75 per cent full, water vapour lands on it and stays. A thin film of salty water forms on the grain. In very damp air, the salt gets wet and clumps. That is why the salt in a kitchen box goes damp in the monsoon. Cooks drop a few grains of rice into a salt box, because dry rice soaks up some of the water and keeps the salt running freely. Sugar and jaggery also pull water from the air, but at higher humidity. Silica gel sachets in shoe boxes are made to pull water from the air, and can take up about a third of their own weight.
examples: Salt in an open dish gets damp and clumpy on a monsoon day.
Jaggery and sugar turn sticky in the damp air of the rainy season.
A silica gel sachet in a shoe box keeps the air inside dry by pulling the water vapour onto itself.
explanations.art: A dish of salt with a thin wet film on the grains and dots from the air landing on them, beside a dry sealed jar.
explanations.context: This card explains why salt turns damp in a humid box, which you see in the Thirsty Things experiment.

explanations.concept: Solids can turn straight into gas
explanations.definition: Sublimation is a solid turning directly into a gas. The reverse, a gas turning directly into a solid such as frost, is called deposition.
explanations.description: A camphor tablet left in the open shrinks and disappears without turning to liquid. Its particles escape straight from the solid into the air, which is why you can smell it. Ice does the same, but very slowly. An ice cube left in a frost-free freezer shrinks over a few days, because its water particles leave as vapour. The vapour then lands on the cold walls as frost. Frozen food that is left unwrapped in a freezer slowly dries out the same way, which is called freezer burn. Cooks and scientists make freeze-dried food by freezing a food and then removing its ice as vapour, so no liquid ever forms.
examples: Camphor tablets shrink in the open, and the smell tells you that the camphor is in the air.
Ice cubes in a freezer shrink over days.
White frost on a freezer wall comes from vapour, not from liquid water.
explanations.art: A camphor tablet beside a smaller one a week later, with wavy smell lines rising, and an ice cube in a freezer with frost forming on the wall.
explanations.context: This card explains how a solid can evaporate, which you watch in the Vanishing Kapoor activity.

explanations.concept: Hot and humid: the wet-bulb limit
explanations.definition: Wet-bulb temperature combines heat and humidity. When it rises too high, sweat cannot evaporate fast enough to cool the body, and the body overheats even in shade.
explanations.description: Sweat cools us only if it evaporates. In very humid air, sweat evaporates slowly, and the body cannot lose enough heat. A wet-bulb thermometer has a wet cloth round its bulb, and it shows how far evaporation can cool something. A day at 35 degrees with 90 per cent humidity is more dangerous than a day at 45 degrees in dry air, because in dry air sweat evaporates freely. Scientists have asked what wet-bulb temperature a healthy person can survive for six hours. They do not agree on the answer. Heat waves in humid parts of India, such as the coast and the Gangetic plain, can come near the dangerous range.
examples: A humid coastal city can feel more dangerous at 38 degrees than a dry desert town at 44.
Outdoor workers in humid heat need shade, water and rest, even if the thermometer reads lower than in a dry heat wave.
A fan helps in dry heat but can be much less useful at very high humidity and temperature.

perspectives.explanation: They calculated that a wet-bulb temperature of about 35 degrees is the limit that even a healthy, resting person in shade could survive for about six hours.

perspectives.who: Later tests with young, healthy volunteers
perspectives.explanation: Experiments in heated rooms found that people began to overheat at wet-bulb temperatures lower than 35 degrees, so the real limit may be lower.

explanations.art: Two people in the heat, one in a dry desert with sweat drying off and one in a humid city with sweat dripping off, and wet-bulb thermometers beside each.
explanations.context: This card explains why humid heat is more dangerous than dry heat at the same air temperature, and where scientists disagree.

explanations.concept: A warmer world carries more water vapour
explanations.definition: For each degree that air warms, it can carry about 7 per cent more water vapour. Warmer air therefore brings heavier downpours and more humid heat.
explanations.description: Because warm air can carry much more water, a warming world sends more water vapour into the air from oceans and wet land. When that air rises in a cloud and cools, more water falls as rain at once. So the heaviest downpours are getting heavier in many places, while the days between them can be longer and drier. Water vapour is also a gas that traps heat, which makes warm air warmer still. Scientists measure these effects by satellite and by weather stations. What they cannot yet say is how clouds will change in each place, and cloud changes are the biggest uncertainty in forecasts of future warming.
examples: Heavy rain events in parts of India have become more frequent, according to weather records.
In many towns, a hot, humid week is followed by a violent thunderstorm.
The same warm sea that feeds a cyclone gives it extra vapour to condense.
explanations.art: A warm sea with more vapour rising into a taller, darker cloud and heavy rain falling on a city.
explanations.context: This card links the numbers for warm air to what is happening to rain and heat in a warming world.

agreed.text: Evaporation takes heat from the liquid left behind, and condensation gives heat out.
agreed.evidence: A drop of sanitiser on your skin feels cold, and the back of a running fridge is warm. William Cullen made a little ice in the 1700s by letting a liquid evaporate fast.

agreed.text: Different liquids evaporate at different speeds, because their particles hold each other with different strengths.
agreed.evidence: On the same plate at the same time, sanitiser dries in seconds, water in minutes, and oil hardly at all.

agreed.text: The most water vapour that air can carry rises quickly with temperature, from about 9 grams in a cubic metre at 10 degrees to about 30 grams at 30 degrees.
agreed.evidence: Weather stations and laboratories have measured this for more than a century. It is why cooling damp air makes dew, fog and cloud.

agreed.text: A liquid boils when its vapour can push back the air, so the boiling point falls on a hill and rises in a pressure cooker.
agreed.evidence: Water boils at about 70 degrees on Mount Everest. A pressure cooker cooks food faster by raising the temperature of the water.

agreed.text: Some substances, such as salt, pull water vapour out of the air without being cold.
agreed.evidence: Salt in a sealed jar stays dry, and salt in a humid box turns damp. Silica gel is made to do the same.

agreed.text: Some solids turn straight into gas without becoming a liquid.
agreed.evidence: Camphor shrinks in the open and leaves a smell. Ice cubes shrink in a freezer, and frost grows on the freezer walls.

challenging.claim: Air is like a sponge that soaks up water, so dry air is thirsty.
challenging.who: A picture in many school books
challenging.for: The picture explains simply why clothes dry in dry air and why damp air feels heavy.
challenging.against: Water also evaporates into an empty space with no air in it. In William Cullen's experiment, a pump took the air away and the liquid still evaporated. The limit on vapour depends on temperature, not on the air being thirsty. The sponge picture is handy but not literally true.
challenging.context: This card tests the idea that air soaks up water like a sponge.

challenging.claim: Boiling and evaporation are the same thing.
challenging.against: Evaporation happens only at the surface, at any temperature, and slowly. Boiling happens throughout the liquid, at one temperature for a given pressure, with bubbles of vapour.
challenging.context: This card tests whether boiling and evaporation are the same.

challenging.claim: A lid makes water boil hotter.
challenging.for: A covered pan comes to the boil sooner and seems to boil harder.
challenging.against: Water in a covered pan still boils at 100 degrees at sea level. The lid keeps the heat and the vapour in, so the pan boils sooner and loses almost no water. Only a pressure cooker, which holds in pressure, makes the water hotter.
challenging.context: This card tests the idea that a lid raises the boiling point.

challenging.claim: A fan makes the room colder.
challenging.for: You feel cooler sitting under a fan.
challenging.against: A thermometer in the room reads the same with the fan on. A fan moves air, which helps your sweat evaporate and takes warm air away from your skin. It cools you, not the room, and its motor adds a little heat.
challenging.context: This card tests whether a fan cools the air.

challenging.claim: Salt gets damp in the monsoon because rain leaks into the box.
challenging.for: The salt gets wet in the rainy season.
challenging.against: Salt in a sealed jar stays dry in the same room. Salt in an open dish gets damp even indoors. The salt is pulling water vapour out of the air.
challenging.context: This card tests where the water on damp salt comes from.

challenging.claim: Ice cubes shrink in the freezer because they melt a little.
challenging.for: Ice cubes do get smaller if you leave them in a freezer for days.
challenging.against: The freezer is below zero, so the ice cannot melt. The ice turns straight into vapour, which then lands on the cold walls as frost.
challenging.context: This card tests why ice cubes shrink in a freezer.

challenging.claim: On a humid day, sweating always cools you.
challenging.for: Sweating is how bodies cool themselves.
challenging.against: Only sweat that evaporates cools you. In humid air, sweat drips off or stays on the skin, and the body loses far less heat. This is why humid heat is more dangerous than dry heat at the same temperature.
challenging.context: This card tests whether sweating always cools.

big_questions.q: In the Drop Race, the sanitiser felt colder on your hand than the water, but both were at room warmth. Where did the cold come from?
big_questions.hint: Think about which particles leave a liquid first, and what they carry with them.

big_questions.q: A pan with a lid loses almost no water, and an open pan loses a lot, yet the water boils at the same temperature in both. What does the lid change?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the vapour meets under the lid.

big_questions.q: Salt is not cold, yet water drops form on it in a damp room. What does this tell you about what makes water vapour turn into a liquid?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a grain of salt does to the water that touches it.

big_questions.q: Camphor shrinks in a box and leaves no puddle. Where does it go, and is it right to say a solid can evaporate?
big_questions.hint: Think about the smell of camphor. What has to reach your nose for you to smell something?

big_questions.q: A fridge keeps food cold by pushing heat out into the kitchen. Can anything be cooled for free?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the heat goes, and what pays for it.

big_questions.q: When sea water evaporates, heat leaves the sea with the vapour. The heat is given out again when the vapour turns into drops in a cloud. Is the monsoon a way of moving heat as much as a way of moving water?
big_questions.hint: Think about the warm sea and the cooler air high above it.

big_questions.q: On a very humid day, a person can overheat even in the shade, with water to drink. What does that say about how a body cools itself?
big_questions.hint: Think about what has to happen to sweat for it to cool you.

big_questions.q: If a warmer world carries more water vapour, could it have more floods and also longer dry spells? How could both be true?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the extra vapour comes down, and how often.

how_we_found_out.story: A wet cloth feels cold, and a clay pot of water stays cool. People knew this for ages. But why? Many thought that cold was something that flowed in from cold air or from a cold thing nearby. Around 1748 (some accounts say 1756), William Cullen, a Scottish doctor who taught at the University of Glasgow, tried a test. He put a dish of ether, a liquid that evaporates very fast, in a jar, and a pump took the air out. With the air gone, the ether boiled away quickly, and the dish and the water around it got so cold that a little of the water froze. No cold air and no cold thing had been brought near. The cold came from the liquid leaving. In the 1800s, inventors used this idea to build the first machines that make ice. Every fridge today works by letting a liquid evaporate.
how_we_found_out.who: William Cullen, a Scottish doctor and teacher at the University of Glasgow
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought that cold was something that flowed in from cold air or cold things. Cullen showed that a liquid can make its own cold, just by evaporating, even when almost all the air has been pumped out.

story.title: The Salt That Knew
story.note: The story is made up. The science is real: salt pulls water vapour out of the air when the humidity is above about three-quarters, and rice vadams cannot dry in air that is nearly full of water. Janani, her family and the week are imagined.
text: It was the last week of May in Kumbakonam, and the terrace was covered with white circles. Janani's family was drying vadams for the whole year. Her mother and her Paati had spent the morning dropping spoonfuls of rice batter onto old cotton saris, in rows and rows, like a field of small white moons.
Janani was nine, and her job was to watch for crows. The sun was strong, the sky was blue, and Appa said the vadams would be ready to store by Thursday.
At eleven o'clock, Paati went down to the kitchen to make coffee. She came back up with her tumbler and a worried face.
'Bring them in,' she said. 'Rain is coming.'
Everyone looked at the sky. It was a clear blue, with only two small clouds.
'There is no rain in that sky,' said Appa. He held up his phone. 'Look. Sunshine. Rain, zero per cent, until six this evening.'
'The salt is wet,' said Paati. 'When the salt in my box goes damp, rain comes before night. My mother knew it, and her mother too.'
Appa smiled kindly, the way grown-ups smile at old sayings. 'Paati, the phone looks at satellites.'
Janani slipped down the stairs to the kitchen. On the shelf stood two things that held salt. One was Paati's old steel box, with its lid off. The other was a glass jar with a tight lid.
She dipped a finger into the steel box. The salt was soft and lumpy, with a wet shine on top. She opened the glass jar. Its salt ran through her fingers like sand.
Same salt. Same shelf. One dry, one damp. The only difference was the lid.

Janani stood very still. When Amma took a cold bottle from the fridge, it grew a coat of drops. That water came from the air. But the salt was not cold. Nothing cold had touched it. So where had its water come from?
She ran back up. 'Appa, what does the phone say about humidity?'
'Eighty-two per cent,' said Appa. 'Why?'
'And yesterday, when the salt was dry?'
Appa scrolled back. 'Fifty-eight.'

Janani counted on her fingers. 'Yesterday, the air was a little over half full of water, and the salt was dry. Today, the air is nearly full, and the salt is wet. So the salt drinks from the air when the air is damp enough.' She took a breath. 'Paati's salt is not telling us about rain. It is telling us about the air. And if the air is nearly full of water, what happens to the vadams?'
Appa opened his mouth, and shut it again.

'They cannot dry,' said Janani. 'The water in the wet vadams has nowhere to go if the air cannot take any more. And when the Sun heats the ground and the damp air goes up, it cools, and the water comes out as clouds. That makes rain.'
There was a pause. Then Paati said, very gently, 'Appa, the saris.'

They carried the vadams in, sari by sari, like sleeping children. Amma laid them on the beds and the dining table. By two o'clock, the sky to the west had turned the colour of a bruise. By four, thunder rolled across the town and the rain came down so hard that the lane flooded in minutes. Across the road, a neighbour ran out in her nightdress, trying to drag a sheet of drying chillies under a roof.
Appa stood at the window, watching. 'The phone said zero,' he said at last.
'The phone was not wrong about the sky,' said Paati. 'It was just late.'

The next day the sun came back, and the vadams dried by afternoon, crisp as paper. That evening, Janani found two small saucers and two spoons of salt. She put one in a jar and left the other on the kitchen shelf. Beside them she placed a notebook. Every morning she wrote one line: dry or damp, and what the phone said about humidity.
After a week, she had a pattern. The open salt went damp every time the number went above about seventy-five.
Paati dropped three grains of rice into her steel box. 'My mother did this,' she said. 'I never asked why.'
'The rice drinks a little of the water too,' said Janani, 'so the salt stays loose.'
Paati laughed until her coffee shook. 'A scientist in the kitchen,' she said.
story.epiphany: For the parent: table salt pulls water vapour out of the air once the relative humidity is above about 75 per cent, even though the salt is not cold. It forms a thin film of salty water on the grains, and the salt clumps. In a sealed jar, the air inside stays drier, so the salt stays loose. A damp salt box is therefore a sign that the air is nearly full of water. Air that damp cannot take much more water from wet vadams, so they dry very slowly, and it is also the kind of air that makes clouds and storms when it rises and cools. The phone saw clear sky at that moment, and the salt felt the air. Dry rice in the salt takes up some of the water, which keeps the salt free-flowing.
ask: Why was the salt in the jar dry, when the salt in the steel box was damp?
The salt was not cold. So where did its water come from?
How did Janani use the numbers from the phone to work out what the salt was telling her?
Why would the vadams not dry, even in sunshine, when the air was almost full of water?
What did Janani do after the storm to check her idea?

roots.context: We have raced liquids across a plate, boiled water with and without a lid, and watched salt pull water from the air. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Drop Race, the drop of sanitiser on your hand vanished fastest and felt the coldest. The drop of water vanished more slowly and felt less cold. Nothing cold touched your skin. The liquid that left took heat from your skin with it.
deep_truth.habit: We think cold is something that arrives, like ice or a cold wind. In the Drop Race, the cold on your hand came from something going away. The liquid left and your skin cooled, and these were one event, not two.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Drop Race, a drop of sanitiser dried in seconds and felt colder on the skin than a drop of water on the same hand. William Cullen froze water by letting a liquid boil away, with nothing cold brought near.

three.who_am_i: When you sweat, water leaves your skin and carries heat away with it. Your body keeps its temperature steady by letting water go.
three.what_is_life: A tulsi plant on a balcony sends water out of their leaves all day. As the water leaves, it cools the leaves and pulls more water up from the roots.
three.what_is_this_world: Water that evaporates from the sea carries the Sun's heat up as vapour, and gives it out again in the clouds. The monsoon moves heat as well as water.

roots.thread: Water takes in a great deal of heat when it becomes a gas, and it gives that heat out when it becomes a liquid again. A drop on your hand, a fridge, a salt box, a monsoon cloud and the sea are all places where heat is taken in or given out in this way. No heat is made or lost. It is carried from one place to another by water changing state, and the same thing happens in every one of those places.

teachings.teaching: Krishna says to Arjuna: 'I give heat. I hold back the rain and I send it forth.' The verse speaks of heat and rain together, as two parts of one act of giving and holding back.
teachings.link: In the monsoon, the Sun's heat lifts water from the sea and the same water falls as rain. Heat and rain are two sides of the same journey of water.

teachings.source: Tirukkural 20, in the chapter on the excellence of rain
teachings.teaching: Thiruvalluvar says that as the world cannot go on without water, so no one's way of life can go on without rain.
teachings.link: Water that evaporated from the sea and condensed in clouds is what fills every river, tank and well. The cycle of leaving and returning is what keeps everything going.

science.text: When a liquid evaporates, it takes heat from what is left, and when vapour condenses it gives the same heat out.
A fridge and an air conditioner use this to move heat from a cold place to a warm place, and tropical storms get much of their power from heat released by condensing vapour.
Exactly how much humid heat a healthy person can survive is still being tested.

other_view.view: Fast particles leave a liquid because they are fast, and the rest are cooler for the same reason. It is a matter of numbers and averages. Calling it 'giving' or 'taking' is a way of speaking, and it does not say that water or heat has any part in a bigger pattern.

practice.title: A cool patch on your hand
practice.say: Wet the back of your hand with one drop of water. Hold it still. Breathe in slowly. Now breathe out gently across your hand, and feel the cool patch. Breathe in again. Breathe out across the patch again. Notice the cool spot get smaller as the water leaves. Do this three times, then sit quietly.
practice.kid: Put a drop of water on the back of your hand. Blow on it gently. Feel it get cool. Breathe slowly three times.

ask: The coldness on your hand came from water leaving. Where do you think your warmth went?
When you sweat, is the water that leaves you still yours? Where is it a day later?
If the monsoon moves heat from the sea to the land, who is carrying it, the wind or the water?

printables.title: 8 bonus question cards, with the answer on the back

items.f: What does a dew point of 24 degrees mean?
items.b: If the air is cooled to 24 degrees, it becomes full of water vapour, and anything colder than 24 gets drops.

items.f: Why is the dew point higher on a hot, damp day than on a cold, damp day?
items.b: Hot air can carry much more vapour. So when hot air and cold air are equally close to full, the hot air holds more water, and its dew point is higher.

items.f: Which has a higher dew point, a hot dry day or a hot damp day?
items.b: A hot damp day, because there is more vapour in the air.

items.f: Why does a steel glass of cold water mist more than a plastic cup of the same water?
items.b: Steel passes the cold of the water to its outside faster, so its outside gets colder than the dew point sooner.

items.f: Why can fog form on a clear, still night?
items.b: The air near the ground cools to its dew point, so its vapour condenses into tiny drops.

items.f: What happens to relative humidity when you warm a closed room without adding water?
items.b: It falls, because the same vapour is now a smaller share of what the warm air could carry.

items.f: Two lots of air are both at 30 degrees. One has a dew point of 22 and the other has a dew point of 28. Which is closer to saturation?
items.b: The air with a dew point of 28, because its dew point is closer to the air temperature.

items.f: Why does the dew point matter more than humidity for knowing if a glass will mist?
items.b: The dew point is a temperature, so you can compare it straight away with the temperature of the glass.

rules: Put the dew point chart where everyone can see it. If you have no printer, copy the chart and the cards onto paper slips. Shuffle the 24 air and glass cards and put them face down. Put the bonus cards in another pile.
On your turn, turn over a card and read it aloud. Find the dew point in the chart for that air temperature and humidity.
Say MIST if the glass is colder than the dew point. Say NO MIST if the glass is warmer. Say the dew point out loud too.
Turn the card over to check. A right answer scores 1 point. If you also said the right dew point, you score 1 more.
After every fourth card, the next player answers a bonus card for 1 point.
If two players disagree, the one who found the dew point first in the chart decides. Then check the back of the card.
After 24 cards, the player with the most points wins. If points are equal, you share the win. If you play alone, try to beat your own score next time.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and the dew point chart. Read the chart together. Find the dew point for air at 30 degrees and 70 per cent humidity.
flow.say: The dew point is the temperature at which the air is full of water vapour. A glass colder than the dew point gets drops. Find the dew point for 30 degrees and 70 per cent humidity in the chart.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and the chart. Find the dew point for 30 degrees and 70 per cent.
flow.parent: The dew point for 30 degrees and 70 per cent is 24. Any glass colder than 24 degrees mists in this air. Make sure every player can find a number on the chart before you start.
flow.context: This is the first step of Will It Mist? You learn to read the dew point chart.

flow.do: Play the first eight cards. After each card, ask the player to say the dew point and whether the glass is colder or warmer.
flow.say: Read the card. Find the dew point. Is the glass colder or warmer? Say MIST or NO MIST. Then we check.
flow.kid: Read the card. Find the dew point. Is the glass colder or warmer? Say MIST or NO MIST.

good: I found the dew point and compared it with the glass.
The glass was colder than the dew point.
The glass was warmer, so no mist.

flow.context: In this step you play the first eight cards and practise the rule.

flow.do: Play the next eight cards, with a bonus card after the fourth and eighth cards.
flow.say: Now we add a bonus question after every fourth card. Which cards are the hardest? Are they the ones where the glass is close to the dew point?
flow.kid: Play eight more cards. Answer a bonus card after every fourth card.
flow.parent: Cards where the glass is within two degrees of the dew point are the hardest. This is realistic. Real glasses are rarely exactly at the dew point.
flow.context: In this step you play eight more cards and answer bonus questions.

flow.do: Play the last eight cards. Add up the points. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Play the last eight cards. Then count your points. Which weather made it easiest for the glass to mist, hot and damp or cool and dry?
flow.kid: Play the last eight cards. Count your points.

check.q: The dew point of the air is 20 degrees. Which glass will get mist?

A glass of water at 25 degrees
Both glasses
check.why: Mist forms on any surface colder than the dew point. At 15 degrees, the glass is colder than 20, so it mists. The glass at 25 degrees is warmer than the dew point, so it stays dry.

experiments.title: Drop Race: which liquid leaves first, and which feels coldest?
experiments.context: This is the main investigation of the unit. You smear six liquids onto a steel plate and find the order in which they dry. You also feel how cold two of them make your skin.
experiments.question: Water, salt water, sugar syrup, vinegar, coconut oil and hand sanitiser: in what order do they leave the plate? And does the faster one feel colder on your skin?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which liquid will dry first? Which will be last, or never? Will the fastest one feel colder on your hand? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every liquid gets a thin streak of the same size on the same plate, in the same room, at the same time. You use a clean stick for each liquid. Only the liquid changes, so any difference in drying comes from the liquid.
results_table: My guess for the order (1 is first)

materials.item: a large, flat, clean steel plate, dry

six small cups holding: plain water; salt water made with a quarter teaspoon of salt in a tablespoon of water; sugar syrup made with a teaspoon of sugar in a tablespoon of water; vinegar; coconut oil; and hand sanitiser (the usual alcohol kind from a medical shop, about Rs 50) poured by a grown-up. About a tablespoon of each
six clean ice-cream sticks or cotton buds, one for each liquid
a phone timer or a clock
paper and a pen to draw the plate and write the times
a dry cloth for wiping

experiments.safety: Hand sanitiser catches fire easily. Keep it well away from the stove, candles and diyas, and put it away when you finish. A grown-up pours it and puts it on the plate. Do not use it on cut skin, and keep it away from the eyes. Do not taste any of the liquids. Use a hand sanitiser that is a thin liquid or spray if you can. A thick gel leaves a film and dries slower.

schedule.what: Guess, smear six streaks on a plate, feel two on your hand, check every two minutes, and write the order.

experiments.record: Fill in the table, a row for each liquid. Draw the plate at the start and at the end, with the streaks. Then write what you think, what you saw, and why.

setup.art: A large steel plate with six small cups around it, each holding a different liquid, and a stick in each cup.
setup.caption: 1. Line up the six cups and the sticks. Draw the plate on paper.

setup.art: A child smearing a thin streak of one liquid onto a steel plate with a stick, the other streaks already in a ring.
setup.caption: 2. Smear a thin streak of each liquid, each in its own place, about a finger long.

setup.art: A child looking at the plate from the side at eye level while a phone timer runs beside it, some streaks already dull and some still shiny.
setup.caption: 3. Check the plate every two minutes. Which streaks have dried?

setup.art: A child with a drop of water on one hand and a drop of sanitiser on the other, blowing gently on each and pulling a face.
setup.caption: 4. Feel one drop of water and one drop of sanitiser on your hand. Which is colder?

flow.do: Show your child the plate and the six cups. Ask for a guess about the order and a reason. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: Here are six liquids. We will smear a thin streak of each on this plate. Which will dry first? Which will be last? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Here are six liquids. Which will dry first? Which will dry last? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think that one will dry first?
good: It smells strong, so it must be escaping fast.
Water dries because it is thin.
Oil will not dry because it is thick.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Many children guess that oil dries fastest because it is thin and runny, or that the sugar syrup dries first because sugar dissolves. Write the guesses at the top of the table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Drop Race. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Dip a stick into the water. 2. Wipe the extra water off on the rim of the cup. 3. Smear a thin streak, about a finger long and a finger wide, on the plate. 4. Do the same for each liquid with its own stick, in its own place. 5. A grown-up does the sanitiser. 6. Start the timer after the last streak.
flow.say: Wipe the extra off the stick, so the streak is thin. Make every streak the same size. Draw where each liquid is on your paper. Start the timer when the last streak is done.
flow.kid: Dip a stick. Wipe off the extra. Smear a thin streak. Do all six. Start the timer.
flow.parent: A thin streak matters. A puddle takes far longer to dry than a thin film. Keep the streaks at least three centimetres apart. Put the plate where it will not be touched, away from a fan or a window draught. With 2 to 4 children: one child smears and one times, or each child smears three liquids on the shared plate and keeps their own results table. Everyone scores the skin test on their own hand. With one child, the parent holds the timer and the sanitiser.

check.q: Why does each liquid get its own clean stick and the same size of streak?
options: So only the liquid changes
So the plate looks neat
So the sticks last longer
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. Here it is the liquid. If one streak were bigger, you would not know whether the liquid or the size made the difference.

flow.context: In this step you smear six thin streaks on the plate, all the same size.

flow.do: 1. Put a drop of plain water on the back of your hand and spread it to the size of a coin. 2. Wait ten seconds. 3. Score how cold it feels, from 0 to 5. 4. Wipe dry and wait one minute. 5. A grown-up puts a drop of sanitiser on the same place. 6. Score again.
flow.say: Put a drop of water on the back of your hand. How cold does it feel, from 0 to 5? Now a grown-up puts a drop of sanitiser on the same place. How cold does that feel? Which left first?
flow.kid: Put a drop of water on your hand. Score how cold it feels. Try sanitiser. Score again.
flow.parent: Skip the sanitiser if your child's skin is cut or sore. Expect the sanitiser to dry in a few seconds and feel much colder than the water. Blowing gently across each drop makes the cool feeling stronger.
flow.context: In this step you feel how cold a drop of water and a drop of sanitiser feel on your skin.

flow.do: 1. Look at the plate every two minutes for twenty minutes. 2. Look from the side, at eye level. 3. Write down the minute when each streak first looks dry, with no shine. 4. If a streak is still shiny at the end, write 'still wet'.
flow.say: Look from the side. A wet streak is shiny. A dry streak is dull. Tell me when each one stops shining. Which went first? Which are still shiny?
flow.kid: Look every two minutes. Wet streaks shine. Dry ones go dull. Write the minute.
flow.parent: On a humid day water may take more than twenty minutes. If so, switch on a fan that blows on the whole plate, so all six dry in the same moving air, and carry on. Sanitiser dries in seconds, and may leave a sticky film if it is a gel. The oil will not dry at all in this time. These times are typical, not promised. In a hot dry room water may dry in about 5 to 10 minutes. In a damp monsoon room it may still be shiny at 20 minutes. Salt water in a very damp room may never fully dry, and may stay glossy. That is a real result, so write it down and say why.
flow.context: In this step you check the plate every two minutes and write when each liquid dries.

flow.do: Fill in the table for all six liquids. Look at what each streak left behind. Touch the dry ones lightly with a clean finger.
flow.say: Tell me the order from first to last. What did each liquid leave behind? Did the salt water and sugar syrup leave something?
flow.kid: Put the liquids in order. What did each one leave behind?
flow.parent: Expect: sanitiser first, then vinegar and water close together, then salt water, which leaves a white crust. Sugar syrup stays sticky for a long time. Oil stays. Dissolved things cannot evaporate, so they stay behind. Write exactly what you saw.
flow.context: In this step you write the order and look at what is left behind.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.parent: These three things are a claim, the evidence for it, and the reasoning. A strong answer: What I think: liquids leave at very different speeds, and the faster one feels colder. What I saw: sanitiser dried first and felt coldest, water took minutes, and oil stayed. Why: the particles of some liquids hold each other loosely so they escape easily, and the escaping particles take heat from the skin. Do not explain it yourself before they have answered.

check.q: Sanitiser dried in seconds and felt colder than water on the skin. What is the best explanation?
options: Its particles escape faster, and the escaping particles carry heat from the skin
It was colder in the bottle
Skin is colder where it is wet
check.why: The sanitiser's particles hold each other weakly, so many escape each second, and each escaping particle takes some heat. It was at room warmth in the bottle, and the skin is not colder just because it is wet. It is colder because something is leaving.

flow.context: In this step you say what you think, what you saw, and why.

experiments.title: Thirsty Things: which kitchen things pull water out of the air?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make a humid box and find out which kitchen things take water from the air without being cold.
experiments.question: Salt, sugar, jaggery, rice, baking soda and puffed rice (murmura): which of them pull water vapour out of very humid air?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which of the six things will get damp in a humid box? Which will stay dry? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Each thing gets the same amount, in the same kind of saucer, in the same box for the same time. A control saucer of salt stays outside the box in a closed jar. Only the thing changes, so any difference comes from the thing.
results_table: What it looked and felt like after the wait
Did it pull water from the air?

materials.item: seven small saucers or small steel katoris (six for the test, one for the control jar)
one level teaspoon each of table salt, white sugar, jaggery powder, dry uncooked rice and baking soda
a handful of puffed rice (murmura), crisp and dry, about one level tablespoon
a big plastic box with a tight lid, large enough to hold the six saucers (a steel dabba or a big steel pot with a lid also works)
a small heat-proof bowl (steel is best), and half a cup of very hot water poured by a grown-up
a small jar with a tight lid, with a saucer of one level teaspoon of table salt inside it
a clean dry spoon, paper and a pen, and a torch
a kitchen scale that reads in grams, and a sealed silica gel sachet, if you have them (optional: weigh the sachet before and after; it gains only a little, and a basic scale may not show it)

experiments.safety: A grown-up pours the hot water and puts the bowl in the box. Steam can scald, so open the lid away from your face. Use water that is very hot, not furiously boiling, if the box is thin plastic. Do not eat the tested things afterwards. Wash your hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Guess, set out six saucers, put them in a steamy box, wait forty minutes and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the six saucers at the end. Then write what you think, what you saw, and why.

setup.art: Six small saucers each with a heap of a different kitchen thing, labelled with paper slips.
setup.caption: 1. Put one level teaspoon of each thing in its own saucer. Label them.

setup.art: A big plastic box with six saucers inside and a small bowl of steaming water in the middle, a grown-up closing the lid.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up puts the saucers and a bowl of hot water in the box and shuts the lid.

setup.art: A closed glass jar containing a saucer of dry salt, standing beside the big box.
setup.caption: 3. Keep a control saucer of salt in a closed jar outside the box.

setup.art: A child lifting the lid of the box and poking a damp, lumpy salt heap with a dry spoon, with other heaps unchanged beside it.
setup.caption: 4. After forty minutes, open the lid. Look and poke each heap with a dry spoon.

flow.do: Show your child the six things. Ask for a guess about each one, and a reason. Write the guesses.
flow.say: Here are six things. We will put them in a very damp box. Which will get damp? Which will stay dry? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Six things go into a damp box. Which will get damp? Which will stay dry? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think salt will get wet, when it is not cold?
good: Water in the air sticks to it.
It will not get wet, because it is not cold.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Many children say that nothing will get wet, because nothing is cold. Write the guesses.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Thirsty Things test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. Put one level teaspoon of each thing in its own saucer. 2. Label each saucer with a paper slip. 3. Put one level teaspoon of salt in a saucer inside the closed jar. 4. If you have a scale, weigh each saucer and write the number.
flow.say: Use level teaspoons, so every heap is the same size. The salt in the jar is our control. It stays in dry air, so we can compare.
flow.kid: Put a level spoon of each thing in a saucer. Label them. Put salt in the closed jar.
flow.parent: For the puffed rice, put a pinch that is still crisp on its own saucer. Wipe the inside of the lid dry before you start. The control tells you whether the room itself is damp enough to affect salt. If the control salt turns damp, it is a very humid day.

check.q: What is the control jar of salt for?
options: To show what salt does in dry air, so you can compare
To make the box more humid
To keep the salt for cooking
check.why: A control shows what happens when the one thing you are testing, the damp air, is missing. If the control salt stays dry while the box salt gets wet, the damp air must be the cause.

flow.context: In this step you set out six saucers and a control jar of salt.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up puts the six saucers into the big box. 2. A grown-up pours half a cup of very hot water into the small bowl. 3. Set the bowl in the box, not touching the saucers. 4. Close the lid tightly. 5. Note the time.
flow.say: A grown-up will put the saucers in the box with a bowl of hot water. The steam fills the box with water vapour. Close the lid tight. Now we wait forty minutes.
flow.kid: A grown-up puts the saucers and hot water in the box. Close the lid. Note the time.
flow.parent: The hot water fills the closed box with water vapour, so the air inside is almost completely full. Do not open the lid during the wait. If you do not have a big box with a lid, use the bathroom after a hot bath with the door closed. Drops of water may form under the lid and fall onto a saucer. A splash makes one wet spot, while a thing that pulls water from the air goes damp all through the heap. Stand the saucers in a ring away from the middle of the lid if you can, and do not count a splash. For 2 to 4 children: one child writes the labels, one sets the timer, and each guesses for every saucer, then compares guesses at the end.
flow.context: In this step a grown-up makes the box humid, with a bowl of hot water and a tight lid.

flow.do: Leave the box closed for forty minutes. Do not open the lid.
flow.say: Now we wait forty minutes. What do you think is happening inside the box?
flow.kid: Wait forty minutes. Do not open the box.
flow.parent: Leave it for forty minutes. A longer wait of an hour gives larger differences. Keep the box away from sunlight.
flow.context: In this step you wait while the humid air works on the six things.

flow.do: 1. Open the lid away from your face. 2. Look at each saucer with a torch. 3. Poke each heap gently with a clean dry spoon. Snap a piece of puffed rice. 4. Write what it looks and feels like: dry and loose, clumpy, sticky or wet. 5. Look at the control salt in the jar.
flow.say: Open the lid slowly. Look at each heap. Poke it with the spoon. Is it loose and dry, or lumpy, sticky or wet? Compare with the control salt.
flow.kid: Open the lid slowly. Look at each heap. Poke it. Dry, lumpy, sticky or wet?
flow.parent: Expect the salt to be clumpy with a wet shine, the jaggery powder to be sticky, the puffed rice to be soft and chewy (snap one piece and listen), and the sugar to be a little tacky. These are typical results, and they depend on the weather. The rice and the baking soda should look about the same as before. The control salt should be dry. If differences are small, leave the box closed for 30 more minutes and look again.
flow.context: In this step you open the box and compare the six heaps with the control.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.parent: A strong answer: What I think: some things pull water out of damp air even when they are not cold. What I saw: the salt and jaggery got damp in the box, while the control salt stayed dry. Why: they hold on to water so strongly that water vapour lands on them and stays. Do not explain it yourself before they have answered.

check.q: The salt in the humid box got damp, but the salt in the closed jar stayed dry. What does this show?
options: The salt pulled water out of the damp air
The box made the salt cold
Salt gets damp when it is old
check.why: The only difference between the two salts was the damp air. So the damp air is the cause. The salt was not cold, and the control salt was just as old, so neither of those could explain the difference.

flow.context: In this step you say what you think, what you saw, and why.

experiments.title: Lid On or Lid Off: how much water leaves a boiling pan?
experiments.context: In this experiment you boil water in two pans, one with a lid and one without, and measure how much water is left. A grown-up does all the cooking, and you measure.
experiments.question: Two pans boil for ten minutes, one with a lid and one without a lid. How much water leaves each one?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which pan will lose more water? How much more? Will the water in the pan with the lid boil hotter or not? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both pans start with the same amount of water at the same warmth. They are heated on the same flame and boil for the same time. Only the lid changes, so any difference comes from the lid.
results_table: Water left after ten minutes of boiling (millilitres)

materials.item: two identical small steel pans, or one pan used twice
one lid that fits the pans
a measuring jug marked in millilitres
one litre of water at room temperature
a stove with a flame that can be set to the same level, and oven gloves or tongs
a phone timer and paper and a pen

experiments.safety: A grown-up does all the cooking. Steam and the lid can burn badly. Tie back long hair and loose dupattas, and keep children at arm's length from the stove. Lift the lid away from your face with oven gloves or tongs. A grown-up pours the water into the jug only once the pan is cool enough to touch with a bare hand, which can take 30 minutes. Then the child reads the level on the jug.

schedule.what: Guess, measure water into two pans, boil for ten minutes with and without a lid, let them cool, then measure the water left.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the underside of the lid after boiling. Then write what you think, what you saw, and why.

setup.art: Two small steel pans on a stove, each with 500 millilitres of water from a measuring jug, one with a lid beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Measure the same amount of water into two pans. Put a lid on only one.

setup.art: The two pans boiling, one with steam rising into the air and one with the lid on and a little steam at its edge.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up boils both pans for ten minutes.

setup.art: The lid being lifted away carefully by a grown-up in oven gloves, with drops on the underside.
setup.caption: 3. Look at the drops under the lid after the heat is off.

setup.art: A child at a table pouring the cooled water from each pan into a measuring jug and reading the level at eye height.
setup.caption: 4. When the pans have cooled, pour each into the jug and read how much is left.

flow.do: Show your child the two pans, the lid and the jug. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess.
flow.say: We will boil two pans of water for ten minutes. One has a lid and one does not. Which will lose more water? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Two pans. One has a lid. Which loses more water? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Where do you think the missing water goes?

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children say the open pan loses more. Some say the pan with a lid will boil hotter. Write the guess and the reason.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Lid On or Lid Off test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up pours 500 millilitres of water into each pan. 2. Check each pan with the jug. 3. Write the starting amount. 4. Put the lid on one pan only.
flow.say: Pour exactly 500 millilitres into each pan. Write it down. The lid goes on one pan only. Everything else is the same.
flow.kid: Measure 500 millilitres into each pan. Write it down. Put the lid on one pan only.
flow.parent: If you only have one burner, do two runs, one after the other, with the same pan, the same flame setting and fresh water at room temperature each time. Let the pan cool before the second run.

check.q: Why do both pans start with exactly the same amount of water?
options: So that only the lid changes
So the pans are easy to carry
So they boil at the same moment
check.why: If one pan had more water, you could not tell if the lid or the amount made the difference. In a fair test, only one thing changes.

flow.context: In this step you measure the water into two pans. Only one gets a lid.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up lights the stove under both pans at the same flame. 2. When the water in the open pan is boiling steadily, start a ten-minute timer. 3. Lower the flame a little if the covered pan bubbles over. 4. After ten minutes, turn the stove off.
flow.say: A grown-up lights both pans. When the open pan boils steadily, we start the ten-minute timer. Stay back and watch the steam. Where does it go in each pan?
flow.kid: A grown-up boils both pans for ten minutes. Stay back. Watch the steam.
flow.parent: Do not lift the lid during the boil. Look at the steam: the open pan sends a cloud of steam into the kitchen, while the covered pan lets out only a little at the edge. The pan with the lid usually reaches a boil sooner. Do not lean over either pan.
flow.context: In this step a grown-up boils both pans for ten minutes while you watch from a safe distance.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up lifts the lid away from your face with oven gloves. 2. Look at the underside of the lid. 3. Look at the sides of the covered pan. 4. Ask your child what the drops are.
flow.say: Look at the underside of the lid. What do you see? Where did those drops come from? What do you think they were a minute ago?
flow.kid: Look under the lid. What do you see? Where did the drops come from?
flow.parent: The drops are condensed water vapour. The vapour hit the cooler lid, turned back into liquid, and ran back into the pan. The open pan has no lid to do this.
flow.context: In this step you look at the drops under the lid.

flow.do: 1. Wait 20 to 30 minutes, until a grown-up finds the pans cool enough to touch with a bare hand. 2. A grown-up pours the water from the open pan into the jug. 3. Read the level at eye height and write it. 4. Do the same with the covered pan. 5. Work out how much each lost.
flow.say: Pour each pan into the jug and read the level at eye height. How much is left in each? Take it away from 500. How much was lost?
flow.kid: Wait until the pans are cool. Pour each into the jug. Read the level. Work out the loss.
flow.parent: Expect the open pan to lose noticeably more, typically about 100 to 250 millilitres in ten minutes of steady boil on a home gas flame (more on a high flame), and the covered pan only a few millilitres. Do not turn the flame to high: the open pan could lose half its water. Your numbers depend on your flame and pan, so write exactly what you measure. Use a steel or heat-proof jug, since the water may still be hot. For 2 to 4 children: one reads each jug, one writes the numbers, and one checks the reading again. With one child, the parent pours and the child reads.
flow.context: In this step you measure how much water is left in each pan.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things: what you think, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.parent: A strong answer: What I think: a lid keeps almost all the water in the pan. What I saw: the open pan lost about ninety millilitres and the covered pan about ten, and there were drops under the lid. Why: the vapour meets the cooler lid, turns back to liquid and drips back. Do not explain it yourself before they have answered.

check.q: The covered pan lost far less water than the open pan. What does this show?
options: Vapour met the cooler lid, turned back into drops and fell into the pan
The water in the covered pan did not boil
The lid made the water boil hotter
check.why: Both pans boiled, as the steady bubbles showed. In the covered pan the vapour had a lid to condense on, and the drops ran back. Water at sea level boils at 100 degrees whether or not there is a lid, so the lid did not make it hotter.

flow.context: In this step you say what you think, what you saw, and why.

activities.title: Fridge Fog: watch a cloud fall out of the freezer
activities.context: This is the first thing to do in the unit. You open the freezer door and watch what pours out, then guess what it is.

materials.item: a fridge with a freezer compartment that has been running for a while
a torch or phone torch
a watch and a pen and paper

schedule.what: Open the freezer door for twenty seconds, watch the fog, shine a torch across it, breathe into the freezer, then close the door.

activities.record: Draw the open freezer and the fog. Show which way the fog moved. Write one sentence saying what you think the fog is.

setup.art: A child standing at an open freezer door in a warm kitchen with a white fog spilling down over the shelf below.
setup.caption: 1. Open the freezer door and watch the air that pours out.

setup.art: A torch beam shining sideways across the fog to show it clearly, with a grown-up holding the door.
setup.caption: 2. Shine a torch across the fog from the side.

setup.art: A child breathing out a white cloud into the cold space of an open freezer.
setup.caption: 3. Breathe out into the freezer. Watch your breath.

flow.do: 1. Stand a metre from the fridge. 2. Ask your child to guess what will happen when the freezer door opens. 3. A grown-up opens the door fully and holds it open for twenty seconds.
flow.say: I will open the freezer door and hold it for twenty seconds. Watch what comes out. Which way does it move? What do you think it is?
flow.kid: A grown-up opens the freezer. Watch for twenty seconds. What comes out? Which way does it go?

ask.q: What do you think the white stuff is?

flow.parent: Do not say what it is. On a humid day, you will see a white fog flow out and fall down towards the floor. On a very dry day, it may be thin or invisible. If you see nothing, try again after a hot bath has run, or on a rainy day.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fridge Fog. You guess before you look.

flow.do: 1. Keep the door open. 2. Shine the torch sideways across the doorway. 3. Watch the fog in the beam. 4. Close the door after twenty seconds.
flow.say: The torch beam shows the fog more clearly. Which way does it flow, up or down? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Shine the torch across the doorway. Which way does the fog go? Up or down?
flow.parent: The fog flows down and out along the bottom of the doorway, because cold air is heavier than warm air. It is a cloud of tiny drops of water, formed when warm room air met the freezer air and cooled below its dew point.
flow.context: In this step you shine a torch across the fog to see which way it moves.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up opens the door again. 2. Breathe out slowly into the cold space. 3. Watch your breath. 4. Close the door.
flow.say: Breathe out slowly into the freezer. What do you see? Where do you think the water in your breath came from?
flow.kid: Breathe out into the freezer. What do you see? Where did the cloud come from?
flow.parent: Your breath carries water vapour from inside you. The cold air cools it below its dew point, and a white cloud of tiny drops appears. It is the same thing that happens on a cold morning when you can see your breath. The breath cloud works even when the fog does not, so the activity never fails. For 2 to 4 children: one child holds the torch and one watches the direction of the fog, then swap and repeat.

check.q: A white fog pours out of a freezer on a humid day. What is the fog?
options: Tiny drops of water that formed when damp warm air met the cold air
Smoke from the fridge motor
Frozen air
check.why: The water vapour in the warm room air cools suddenly when it meets the freezer air. It condenses into drops too small to see one by one, and together they look like a white fog. It is not smoke, and air does not freeze into fog.

flow.context: In this step you breathe into the freezer and decide what the fog is.

activities.safety: A grown-up opens and holds the freezer door. Keep fingers away from the door edge. Do not put your head inside. Close the door after the activity so the food does not warm up.

activities.title: Feel the Heat Leave: the back of a fridge and an air conditioner
activities.context: In this activity you find out where the heat from the inside of a fridge goes, by feeling the warmth around it.

materials.item: a fridge that has been running for several hours
an air conditioner with an outdoor unit that a grown-up can reach safely (if your home has one)
paper and a pen

activities.safety: A grown-up checks that the back is safe to reach. Do not pull a heavy fridge away from the wall. Do not touch the coils or any fan. Hold the back of your hand a few centimetres away from the surface, not on it. Do not climb to reach an outdoor air conditioner.

schedule.what: Feel the air near the inside, the front and the back of a running fridge, and near an outdoor air conditioner.

activities.record: Draw the fridge and mark the cool places in blue and the warm places in red. Write one sentence saying where you think the heat from inside goes.

setup.art: A child holding the back of a hand near the inside shelf of an open fridge and feeling the cold.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the back of your hand near the inside of the fridge. Feel the cold.

setup.art: A child holding the back of a hand a few centimetres from the grille at the back of the fridge, with red warm waves.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the back of your hand near the back of the fridge. Feel the warmth.

setup.art: An outdoor air conditioner box on a wall with warm air blowing out of it, and a grown-up pointing.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up shows the outdoor box of an air conditioner. Feel the air from it.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child where the heat taken out of the food goes. 2. Let them feel the cold near the inside of the fridge.
