flow.say: A fridge makes the inside cold. But heat does not just disappear. Where do you think the heat from the food goes? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A fridge makes the inside cold. Where does the heat go? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Where do you think the heat from inside the fridge goes?

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children think the heat just disappears.
flow.context: This is the first step of Feel the Heat Leave. You guess where the heat goes.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up checks that the back or side of the fridge is safe to reach. 2. Hold the back of your hand 5 centimetres from the back or side panel. 3. Move it across and feel the warmth. 4. Compare with the air in front of the fridge. 5. Score the warmth from 0 to 5 at the front, side and back. Write the scores.
flow.say: Hold the back of your hand a few centimetres away. Do not touch it. Is it warmer here than at the front? Which part is warmest?
flow.kid: Hold your hand near the back of the fridge. Do not touch. Is it warm? Where is it warmest?
flow.parent: Hold the hand near the side panel too, as many fridges have their warm pipe there. The warmth is gentle, not hot. If you cannot reach the back of the fridge, feel the warm air that comes out at the gap above or below it. For 2 to 4 children: each child scores the warmth, and they compare scores. If the scores differ, try again with every hand at the same distance.
flow.context: In this step you feel the warmth coming from the back of the fridge.

flow.do: If your home has an air conditioner, a grown-up shows your child the outdoor box. Your child feels the air from it with the back of the hand, from a safe distance.
flow.say: The air conditioner makes your room cool. Feel the air from the box outside. Is it warm or cool? Where did that heat come from?
flow.kid: Feel the air from the box outside. Is it warm or cool? Where did the heat come from?
flow.parent: The outdoor box blows warm air, because it gives out the heat taken from the room, plus the heat of the motor. A fridge works the same way on a smaller scale.

check.q: Why is the back of a running fridge warm?
options: The fridge moves heat from the inside to the back, where it is given out to the room
The fridge motor is the only warm part
Heat from inside the food just disappears
check.why: A fridge takes heat from inside and gives it out at the back, where the special liquid condenses. The motor adds a little heat too, but the main warmth is the heat taken from the food. Heat never just disappears.

flow.context: In this step you feel the air from an outdoor air conditioner, if your home has one, and answer the question.

activities.title: Predict the Sweat: will a glass mist today?
activities.context: In this activity you use the dew point from a weather app to predict whether a glass of water will mist, and then you test your prediction.

materials.item: a phone with a weather app that shows the dew point, or the temperature and humidity (for the chart in the Will It Mist? game)
three steel tumblers or glasses (clear glass shows the mist best)
tap water, water from the fridge, and ice cubes
a dry cloth, a spoon, paper and a pen

schedule.what: Find today's dew point, predict whether three glasses will mist, test them, and compare.

activities.record: Write the air temperature and dew point. Draw a table with three glasses: tap water, fridge water and ice water. Write your prediction, the result, and the glass temperature if you can measure it.

setup.art: A phone showing the weather with temperature, humidity and dew point, held next to three steel tumblers.
setup.caption: 1. Find today's dew point on a weather app.

setup.art: Three steel tumblers: one with tap water, one with fridge water and one with ice water, side by side.
setup.caption: 2. Fill three tumblers with tap water, fridge water and ice water.

setup.art: A child wiping the outside of a tumbler dry with a cloth, then watching for mist.
setup.caption: 3. Wipe each tumbler dry. Watch for mist for two minutes.

flow.do: 1. Open the weather app. 2. Find the air temperature and the dew point. If the app shows only humidity, use the dew point chart from the game. 3. Write them both down.
flow.say: Find the air temperature and the dew point. The dew point is the temperature at which the air is full of water vapour. A glass colder than it gets mist. Write both numbers.
flow.kid: Find the temperature and the dew point on the weather app. Write both numbers.
flow.parent: Dew points in India vary widely. On a humid coastal day it may be 24 to 27. On a winter morning in the north it may be below 10. If the app shows only humidity, look up the dew point in the chart from the Will It Mist? game.
flow.context: This is the first step of Predict the Sweat. You find the dew point.

flow.do: 1. Fill one tumbler with tap water. 2. Fill one with fridge water. 3. Fill one with water and plenty of ice cubes. 4. Ask your child to predict which will mist and which will stay dry, comparing each water's warmth with the dew point.
flow.say: Tap water is about as warm as the room. Fridge water is much colder. Ice water is colder still. Compare each one with the dew point. Which will mist? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which glasses will mist. Compare each with the dew point. Why?

ask.q: Which glass do you think will mist, and which will stay dry?
good: The tap water will stay dry because it is warmer than the dew point.
The fridge glass will mist if it is colder than the dew point.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Tap water in summer is usually 25 to 30 degrees, which may be above or below the dew point on a humid day. Fridge water is often about 8 to 10 degrees. Ice water is nearly 0.
flow.context: In this step you fill three glasses and predict which will mist.

flow.do: 1. Wipe the outside of each tumbler dry. 2. Watch each one for two minutes. 3. Write whether it misted, and how soon. 4. Compare with your predictions. 5. Wipe one misted patch with a finger. If it mists again, the water came from the air, not from a leak.
flow.say: Wipe each tumbler dry. Watch for two minutes. Does mist appear? How soon? Was your prediction right?
flow.kid: Wipe each tumbler dry. Watch for two minutes. Does mist appear?
flow.parent: A glass colder than the dew point will mist within a minute. A glass warmer than it will stay dry. If the tap-water glass is only slightly warmer, add one ice cube at a time and stir. The mist should start when the water has cooled just below the dew point. If you have a thermometer, read the water temperature at that moment. The mist test works with steel tumblers too. The steel just goes dull. For 2 to 4 children: each child takes one glass and makes the prediction before the others see the result. If the weather app shows only humidity, use the dew point chart from the Will It Mist? game.

check.q: The dew point is 23 degrees. Which glass of water will mist?
options: Water at 15 degrees
Water at 28 degrees
Neither will mist
check.why: Mist forms on any surface colder than the dew point. At 15 degrees the glass is colder than 23, so it mists. At 28 degrees it is warmer, so it stays dry.

flow.context: In this step you test the three glasses and compare the results with your predictions.

activities.title: Flat-Bottomed Clouds: how high is the bottom of a cloud?
activities.context: In this activity you guess how high the flat bottoms of clouds are, using the temperature and the dew point from a weather app.

materials.item: a phone with a weather app that shows the temperature and the dew point
a pencil and paper, and a window or balcony with a view of the sky

activities.safety: Never look straight at the Sun. A grown-up stays with the child on a balcony or roof and keeps away from the edge.

schedule.what: On a warm afternoon, find the temperature and dew point, work out the cloud base, and look at the clouds.

activities.record: Write the temperature, the dew point and your cloud base height. Draw the sky with the flat-bottomed clouds.

setup.art: A child at a window looking at a row of small white clouds with flat dark bottoms at the same height.
setup.caption: 1. Look for clouds with flat bottoms on a warm afternoon.

setup.art: A phone showing temperature 32 and dew point 22, and a child writing a sum on paper.
setup.caption: 2. Find the temperature and the dew point. Work out the cloud base.

flow.do: 1. On a warm afternoon, look at the sky. 2. Look for small clouds with flat dark bottoms. 3. Ask your child why the bottoms might be flat and at the same height.
flow.say: Look at the clouds. Their bottoms are flat and all at the same height. Why do you think that is?
flow.kid: Look at the clouds. Their bottoms are flat. Why do you think that is?

ask.q: Why do you think the bottoms are flat and at the same height?
good: The air is the same at that height.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. If the sky is clear or overcast, skip to the next step, where you work out the height. Flat bottoms are easiest to see on a sunny afternoon with small, separate clouds.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Flat-Bottomed Clouds activity. You look at the sky and guess.

flow.do: 1. Read the temperature and the dew point on the weather app. 2. Subtract the dew point from the temperature. 3. Multiply by 125. The answer is roughly the height of the cloud bottoms in metres. It is not exact.
flow.say: Take the dew point away from the temperature. Then multiply by 125. That gives the height of a cloud bottom in metres. For 32 degrees and a dew point of 22, what do you get?
flow.kid: Temperature minus dew point. Multiply by 125. That is the cloud height in metres.
flow.parent: For 32 degrees and a dew point of 22, 32 take away 22 is 10, and 10 times 125 is 1250 metres. This is a rule of thumb for clouds made by warm air rising on a sunny day. It gives an estimate, not an exact height.
flow.context: In this step you work out how high the cloud bottoms are from two numbers.

flow.do: 1. Talk about the answer. 2. A 30-floor building is about 100 metres tall. How many of them would you stack to reach the cloud bottom? 3. Explain why the bottoms are flat. 4. Do the sum again early next morning. Compare. Which gives lower cloud bottoms? Why?
flow.say: A 30-floor building is about 100 metres. How many would you stack to reach the cloud bottoms? Why are the bottoms flat? What happens to rising air as it climbs?
flow.kid: How many tall buildings would reach the cloud? Why are the bottoms flat?
flow.parent: Warm air rises and cools as it climbs. At the height where it has cooled to its dew point, its vapour condenses into drops, and a cloud begins. Every rising bubble of air cools to its dew point at about the same height, so the bottoms are flat. The early-morning sum is usually smaller because the air is closer to its dew point. For 2 to 4 children: each works out the sum alone and the answers are compared. On cloudy or rainy days the rule does not fit, so use it only on a sunny afternoon with small clouds.

check.q: Why do fair-weather clouds have flat bottoms at the same height?
options: Rising air has cooled to its dew point at that height, so drops begin to form there
Wind cuts the bottoms flat
The Sun melts the bottoms
check.why: Rising air cools as it climbs. At one particular height it reaches its dew point, and the water vapour condenses into drops. That height is nearly the same over a wide area, so the bottoms are level. Wind does not cut clouds flat, and the Sun does not melt them.

flow.context: In this step you picture how high the cloud base is and explain why it is flat.

activities.title: The Vanishing Kapoor: a solid that evaporates
activities.context: In this activity you watch a camphor tablet shrink over a week in the open and in a closed jar, and find out how a solid can turn into a gas.

materials.item: two camphor tablets from a pooja shop, the same size
two saucers and one small glass jar with a tight lid
a sheet of white paper, a pencil and a ruler

activities.safety: Camphor is poisonous if swallowed, and it catches fire easily. A grown-up puts the tablets out of reach of little children and keeps them away from flames. Do not sniff the tablets or the open jar closely, and keep them away from anyone with asthma. Do not burn camphor indoors without a grown-up. Wash your hands after touching it. Only a grown-up opens the jar. Keep the saucer away from the pooja diya. Do not use edible camphor for this.

schedule.what: Draw the outline of each tablet, smell them, and put one in the open and one in the closed jar.
Compare the size of both tablets with the outlines.
Measure again, look inside the jar, and say what happened.

activities.record: Draw the outlines on day 1, day 4 and day 7 for each tablet. Write the width in millimetres each time. Write what you saw on the inside wall of the jar.

setup.art: Two camphor tablets on white paper with a pencil outline drawn around each and a ruler beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Draw around each tablet and measure it.

setup.art: One tablet on an open saucer on a shelf and one in a closed glass jar, with smell lines rising from the open one.
setup.caption: 2. Put one tablet in the open and one in a closed jar.

setup.art: The same two tablets a week later, the open one much smaller, and fine white crystals on the inside wall of the jar.
setup.caption: 3. A week later, look and measure again.

flow.do: 1. Place each tablet on the paper and draw around it. 2. Measure the width and write it down. 3. Smell both from a distance. 4. Put one tablet on an open saucer on a shelf. 5. Put the other in the jar and close the lid. 6. Ask your child to predict what will happen to each.
flow.say: These tablets are solid. One will sit in the open and one in a closed jar. After a week, what will each look like? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Draw around each tablet. Measure it. Put one in the open and one in a jar. Guess what happens.

ask.q: What do you think will happen to the tablet in the open? And the one in the jar?

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Keep the tablets away from little children. A camphor tablet does not melt. It slowly turns to gas, and you can smell this. For 2 to 4 children: each child draws round one tablet pair; or one pair is shared and children take turns to measure. In a damp or cool place the change is slow, so a week may show only a few millimetres; wait until day 10 if so. The crystals in the jar are small and may show only on the cool lid.
flow.context: This is the first day of The Vanishing Kapoor. You set it up.

flow.do: 1. Put each tablet back on its outline. 2. Look at the edges. 3. Measure the width. 4. Write the numbers.
flow.say: Put each tablet back on its outline. Has either one shrunk? Which one?
flow.kid: Put each tablet on its outline. Has it shrunk? Which one?
flow.parent: The open tablet usually shrinks and goes slightly rounded at the edges. The jar tablet shrinks less. If you see no change in either, wait until day 7.
flow.context: On day 4 you compare the tablets with their outlines.

flow.do: 1. Measure both tablets again. 2. Look at the inside wall and lid of the jar. 3. Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Measure both tablets again. Look at the inside of the jar. What do you see? What do you think happened to the tablet in the open? Where did it go?
flow.kid: Measure both tablets. Look inside the jar. What happened? Where did the camphor go?
flow.parent: The open tablet should be clearly smaller, because camphor turns straight into a gas, which spreads through the room. In the jar, the gas cannot get away, so it settles again on the cool glass as tiny white crystals. This is a solid turning to gas and back, with no liquid in between.

check.q: A camphor tablet in the open gets smaller and leaves no puddle. What has happened to the camphor?
options: It has turned straight into a gas and spread through the air
It has melted into the shelf
It has turned into water
check.why: Camphor turns directly from a solid into a gas, which is called sublimation. That is why you can smell it. There was no puddle, so it did not melt, and it did not become water.

flow.context: On day 7 you measure the tablets, look inside the jar and say what happened.

projects.title: Evaporation Pan: how many millimetres does the Sun take each day?
projects.context: In this project you measure how much water leaves two jars every day for a week, one in the sun and one in the shade, and draw a line graph.

materials.item: two identical clear straight-sided jars or cut plastic bottles, about 8 centimetres wide
two pieces of thin cotton cloth and two rubber bands
a ruler with millimetres and a marker
water to fill each jar to a depth of 60 millimetres
squared paper, a pen and a pencil

projects.safety: Standing water can let mosquitoes breed, so keep a cloth tied over each jar and empty both jars when the project ends. Keep the jars out of reach of small children.

schedule.what: Fill both jars to 60 millimetres, cover them, and put one in the sun and one in the shade.
Measure the depth in each jar at the same time as day 1, and write the weather.
Measure the depth in each jar and write the weather.
Measure the depth in each jar and write the weather.
Measure the depth in each jar and write the weather.
Measure the depth in each jar and write the weather.
Measure, then draw the line graph and say what you found.

projects.record: Make a table with the day, the depth in the sunny jar, the depth in the shaded jar and the weather. Then draw a line graph with two lines, one for each jar.

setup.art: Two identical jars each with 60 millimetres of water, a ruler measuring the depth, and a cloth tied over the mouth of each.
setup.caption: 1. Fill both jars to 60 millimetres. Tie a cloth over each mouth.

setup.art: One jar on a sunny balcony ledge under a roof, and one on a shelf in a shady room.
setup.caption: 2. Put one jar in the sun and one in the shade, away from rain.

setup.art: A child reading the ruler against the water level in the jar every morning and writing the number in a table.
setup.caption: 3. Measure the depth at the same time every day.

setup.art: A line graph with two lines, falling faster for the sunny jar and slower for the shaded jar.
setup.caption: 4. Draw a line graph of both jars.

flow.do: 1. Pour water into each jar until it is 60 millimetres deep. 2. Tie a cloth over the mouth of each jar with a rubber band. 3. Put one jar on a sunny ledge under a roof, so rain cannot fall in. 4. Put the other in a shady room. 5. Ask your child to predict how much each jar will lose.
flow.say: We will measure the water in two jars every day for a week. One is in the sun and one in the shade. How many millimetres will each lose in a day? Which will lose more? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Fill two jars to 60 millimetres. Cover each with a cloth. Put one in the sun and one in the shade. Guess how much each will lose.

ask.q: Why do you think the sunny jar will lose more water?
good: The Sun is hot, so the water leaves faster.

flow.parent: The cloth keeps mosquitoes from laying eggs in standing water, which matters in India. The cloth lets vapour through but slows it, so losses with the cloth are typically about 1 to 4 millimetres a day on a sunny ledge and under 1 to 2 in a shady room. In the monsoon the loss may be under 1 millimetre a day. Use the same cloth for both jars so that it is a fair test. Do not put the jar where rain can fall into it. If the sunny jar falls below 15 millimetres, stop and graph what you have.
flow.context: This is the first day of the Evaporation Pan. You set up two jars.

flow.wait: Measure once each day, at the same time
flow.do: 1. Lift the cloth. 2. Press the ruler gently to the bottom of each jar. 3. Read the depth in millimetres at eye level and write it in the table. 4. Tie the cloth back. 5. Write the weather: sunny, cloudy, windy or rainy.
flow.say: Measure the depth in each jar, at the same time as yesterday. How many millimetres have gone? What was the weather like?
flow.kid: Measure the depth in each jar. Write it in the table. Write the weather.
flow.parent: Measure at the same time each day, so that each reading is for 24 hours. If a day is missed, measure the next day and record two days. Wet the ruler's end only, not the whole ruler. For 2 to 4 children: one child reads each jar, one writes, and the roles change daily. If the readings differ by about a millimetre, read again. With one child, a parent holds the jar.
flow.context: On each day of the week you measure the water in both jars.

flow.do: 1. On the last day, measure the jars. 2. Work out how many millimetres each lost in the week. 3. Draw a line graph with the days along the bottom and the depth up the side. 4. Draw one line for each jar. 5. Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Draw a line for each jar. Which line falls faster? Which days did the sunny jar lose the most? What was the weather on those days? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Draw a line graph for each jar. Which line falls faster? Why do you think so?
flow.parent: A strong answer: the sunny jar lost more, because warmth and moving air make water leave faster. The days with the biggest losses were the hottest and driest. The line for the shaded jar falls more slowly. A rainy or very humid day will show a small loss for both jars. Weather stations use a wider pan in the same way to measure how much water the sun takes from the land.

check.q: The line for the sunny jar fell faster than the line for the shaded jar. What does this show?
options: Warmth and moving air make water leave faster
Sunshine makes water heavy
The shaded jar had more water at the start
check.why: Both jars started with the same depth of water, so the faster fall in the sunny jar is due to the sun and the breeze. Warmth makes more water particles escape each second, and moving air carries the vapour away.

flow.context: On the last day you graph the results and say what you found.

challenges.title: Keep the Salt Free-Flowing: design a salt box for the monsoon
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. In the rainy season, the salt in many kitchens goes damp and lumpy. You design a way to keep salt loose, and test it in a humid box.
challenges.problem: Keep one level teaspoon of table salt loose and dry for forty minutes inside a very humid box, using only things from home. Compare your design with a plain open saucer of salt.
challenges.safety: A grown-up pours the hot water and opens the lid away from the face, because steam can scald. Do not taste the salt after the test.
constraints: The salt must still be easy to pour at the end.
Use one level teaspoon of salt for each design.
A grown-up pours the hot water into the box.
Every design is tested at the same time in the same box.
materials: table salt, one level teaspoon for each design, and one for a plain open saucer
small jars, katoris, saucers and lids
dry uncooked rice, thin cotton cloth, tissue paper, cling film, foil, a plastic bag and rubber bands
a big plastic box with a tight lid, a small bowl, and half a cup of very hot water poured by a grown-up
general: Put the salt in a jar with a tight lid, so humid air cannot get at it.
Mix a few dry grains of rice into the salt, so the rice takes up some of the water.
Cover the saucer with foil or cling film and press it tightly round the edge.
Keep the salt in a small closed jar inside a bigger closed jar.
creative: Put a layer of dry rice at the bottom of a jar and the salt on top, with a cloth between them.
Wrap the salt in tissue paper inside a tight plastic bag, with a silica gel sachet from a shoe box, if you have one.
Use a lid and a dry rice layer together, and compare with the lid alone.
Test two designs that differ in only one way, such as with rice and without rice.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch two or three designs. Build them and test them in the humid box for forty minutes. Which kept the salt loosest? Which left it dampest? Why do you think so? What would you change next time?

setup.art: Three small jars on a table: one with a tight lid, one with salt and rice, one covered with foil, beside a plain open saucer of salt.
setup.caption: 1. Plan two or three designs and set out a plain saucer of salt as the control.

setup.art: The big plastic box with the designs inside, a bowl of steaming water in the middle and the lid closing.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up puts all designs and the control in the humid box.

setup.art: The box opened after forty minutes, with the control salt damp and lumpy and the best design loose and dry.
setup.caption: 3. Open the box and compare each design with the control.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem together. 2. Ask your child to sketch two or three designs. 3. Ask for the reason for each design.
flow.say: Salt gets damp because it pulls water vapour out of the air. How could you stop the vapour reaching the salt, or take it away before it reaches the salt? Draw some ideas.
flow.kid: Salt pulls water from damp air. How can you stop it? Draw two or three ideas.

ask.q: How would your design keep the salt dry?
good: A tight lid stops the damp air getting in.
Rice takes up some of the water.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Keep the Salt Free-Flowing challenge. You plan your designs.

flow.do: 1. Build each design with one level teaspoon of salt. 2. Label each one. 3. Set out the plain open saucer of salt as the control. 4. Write what each design is.
flow.say: Build your designs. Use one level teaspoon of salt each. Label them. The plain open saucer is the control.
flow.kid: Build your designs. Put one spoon of salt in each. Label them. Set out a plain saucer.
flow.parent: Keep the designs simple. Change one thing at a time, so the result is easier to understand. A plain open saucer in the box is the control.
flow.context: In this step you build your designs and set out the control.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up pours half a cup of hot water into a small bowl. 2. Put all designs, the control and the bowl in the box. 3. Close the lid tightly. 4. Wait forty minutes. 5. Open the lid away from your face.
flow.say: A grown-up pours the hot water. Close the lid tight. We wait forty minutes. Which design do you think will keep the salt loosest?
flow.kid: A grown-up pours hot water into the box. Close the lid. Wait forty minutes.
flow.parent: Do not open the lid during the wait. Steam can scald when you open the lid, so lift it away from your face. If you have no big box, use a bathroom after a hot bath with the door closed.
flow.context: In this step all the designs go into the humid box for forty minutes.

flow.do: 1. Open the box. 2. Look at the control. 3. Poke each design's salt with a dry spoon. 4. Write which stayed loose and which clumped. 5. Say why.
flow.say: Look at the control first. Is it damp? Now each design. Which kept the salt loosest? Which was the worst? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the control. Poke each salt. Which stayed loose? Which clumped? Why?
flow.parent: Expect the control salt to be damp, clumped or even wet. A tight jar lid usually keeps salt dry. A cloth or tissue alone usually does not. A strong answer says that the best designs stopped vapour from reaching the salt or took up the water before the salt did.

check.q: A salt jar with a tight lid stays dry while an open saucer of salt in the same box goes damp. What does this show?
options: The lid stopped water vapour reaching the salt
The jar kept the salt cold
Jars stop salt dissolving
check.why: The salt is the same, and both were in the same humid air. Only the lid changed. The lid kept the vapour away from the salt, so it stayed dry. The jar did not make the salt colder, and dissolving has nothing to do with it.

flow.context: In this step you open the box and compare all your designs with the control.

worksheets.title: Fast Liquids, Cold Skin and Damp Salt (core)

items.p: Which of these liquids evaporates fastest at normal room warmth?
opts: Hand sanitiser
Plain water
Sugar syrup
Coconut oil
items.why: The alcohol in sanitiser has particles that hold each other weakly, so many escape each second. Water is slower, syrup slower still, and coconut oil hardly evaporates at all.

items.p: Hand sanitiser feels cold on your skin because it was kept in the fridge.
items.why: False. Sanitiser at room warmth feels colder than water because it evaporates faster, and the escaping particles take heat from your skin.

items.p: When a liquid evaporates from your skin, the skin gets ____.
items.why: The fastest particles leave and take heat with them, so the skin loses heat and gets cooler.

items.p: Sort these. Does each one take heat in or give heat out?
items: steam turning into drops on a cold lid
a wet streak drying on a plate
vapour condensing at the back of a fridge
items.a: see items
items.why: Evaporation takes heat in from what is left behind. Condensation gives heat out to what is around it.

items.p: Why does a boiling pan with a lid lose much less water than a boiling pan without a lid?
opts: The vapour meets the cooler lid, turns back into drops and falls back into the pan
The water under a lid does not boil
A lid makes the water heavier
items.why: Both pans boil. Under a lid, the vapour condenses on the cooler lid and drips back. Without a lid, the vapour drifts away.

items.p: A pan of water is boiling on the stove. Explain why turning the flame up does not make the water hotter than 100 degrees at sea level.
items.a: Water cannot get hotter than its boiling point in an open pan. The extra heat just makes it boil faster, so more water turns into vapour and the water boils away sooner.
items.why: A strong answer says that boiling holds the temperature at the boiling point, and that the extra heat turns more water into vapour.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: how full the air is of water vapour
the temperature at which air is completely full of vapour
a solid turning straight into a gas
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These four words come up all through the unit.

items.p: Air has a relative humidity of 100 per cent. What does that mean?
opts: The air is carrying all the water vapour it can at its temperature
The air is made of water
The air is at 100 degrees
items.why: Relative humidity compares the vapour in the air with the most it could carry at that temperature. At 100 per cent, the air is full.

items.p: Put the steps of the Lid On or Lid Off test in order.
items: Boil both pans for ten minutes
Pour each pan into a jug and read the level
Measure the same amount of water into two pans
Put a lid on one pan only
a: Measure the same amount of water into two pans
Put a lid on one pan only
Boil both pans for ten minutes
Pour each pan into a jug and read the level
items.why: First give both pans the same start. Then change only the lid. Then boil for the same time. Last, measure what is left.

items.p: Salt in an open dish goes damp on a monsoon day, but salt in a closed jar stays dry in the same room. Why?
opts: Salt pulls water vapour out of damp air when the humidity is high enough
Rain gets into open dishes only
Salt is colder in a dish
items.why: Salt holds water so strongly that water vapour lands on it and stays when the air is damp. The closed jar keeps the damp air away from the salt.

items.p: A fan makes the air in a room colder.
items.why: False. A fan only moves air. It cools you by helping your sweat evaporate and by taking warm air away from your skin. A thermometer in the room reads the same.

items.p: Which one does not pull water out of damp air?
opts: Table salt
Jaggery powder
Silica gel
A steel spoon
items.why: Salt, jaggery and silica gel all hold on to water and take it from damp air. A steel spoon does not.

items.p: Draw a pan of boiling water with a lid on. Show the vapour rising, the drops under the lid, and the drops falling back.
items.a: A pan with a lid, arrows of vapour rising from the water, drops on the underside of the lid, and drops falling back into the water.
items.why: The drawing should show that the same water leaves the pan and comes back to it, so the level hardly changes.
items.art: An empty outline of a pan with a lid on a stove.

items.p: Label the fridge drawing: the cold part inside, the warm part at the back, the liquid evaporating, the liquid condensing.
items.a: The cold pipe inside labelled evaporating, where heat is taken in. The warm pipe at the back labelled condensing, where heat is given out.
items.why: A fridge takes heat in where the liquid evaporates inside and gives it out where the liquid condenses at the back.
items.art: A fridge outline with a loop of pipe inside and at the back, and four blank label lines.

items.p: On a humid day, a white fog pours out when you open the freezer door. Explain what the fog is and where its water came from.
items.a: The fog is tiny drops of water. Water vapour in the warm room air met the cold freezer air and cooled below its dew point, so it condensed into drops.
items.why: A strong answer says the fog is liquid drops, and that the water came from vapour in the room's air.

items.p: The salt in a family's kitchen box goes lumpy every monsoon. Three people in the family suggest how to keep it loose.

views.says: Keep the salt in the fridge, where it is cold.
Keep it in a box with a tight lid and drop in a few grains of dry rice.
Put the salt in the sun for a day every week to dry it.

items.ask: Whose way would you choose? Give a reason from what you know about salt and damp air. Then say one good point about another way.
items.a: A strong answer picks the grandmother's way, because a tight lid keeps damp air away from the salt and the rice takes up some water. A fair point about the brother's way is that drying does work, but the salt gets damp again soon. The father's way is the weakest, because the inside of a fridge is humid, and salt taken out into warm damp air still gets wet.
items.why: Each idea has some use. The best one stops vapour reaching the salt and takes up the water that gets in. A good answer weighs the others fairly.

items.p: The air temperature is 30 degrees and the dew point is 24 degrees. Which glass of water will get mist on its outside?
opts: A glass of water at 22 degrees
A glass of water at 28 degrees
Neither will mist
items.why: Mist forms on any surface colder than the dew point. At 22 degrees the glass is colder than 24, so it mists. At 28 degrees it is warmer, so it stays dry.

items.p: A cubic metre of air at 30 degrees Celsius can carry at most about 30 grams of water vapour. If the air is at 50 per cent humidity, about how many grams of vapour are in each cubic metre?
items.why: 50 per cent is a half. Half of 30 is 15 grams.

items.p: Explain why 35 degrees with very damp air can be more dangerous for a person than 45 degrees with very dry air.
items.a: Sweat cools the body only when it evaporates. In very damp air, sweat evaporates slowly or not at all, so the body cannot lose enough heat. In dry air, sweat evaporates quickly and the body keeps cooler, even at a higher temperature.
items.why: A strong answer links sweat, evaporation and how full the air is with vapour.

items.p: Water in an open pan on a bigger flame boils at a higher temperature.
items.why: False. Water in an open pan cannot get hotter than its boiling point. A bigger flame only makes it boil away faster.

items.p: Water boils at about 92 degrees at Ooty, which is high in the hills. Why is it lower than 100 degrees?
opts: The air presses less on the water, so its vapour can form bubbles at a lower temperature
The air is colder, so the water is colder
The water has less salt
items.why: Boiling happens when the vapour can push back the air. High up, the air presses less, so water boils at a lower temperature. Rice takes longer to cook at Ooty for this reason.

items.p: Sort these. Does each one raise the boiling point of water, lower it, or leave it the same?
items: putting a lid on an open pan
items.a: see items
items.why: A pressure cooker raises the pressure, so water boils hotter. A hill lowers the pressure, so water boils cooler. A lid on an open pan and a bigger flame do not change the boiling point.

items.p: You want to find out which of two liquids evaporates faster. Write a fair test. Say what you will keep the same and what you will change.
items.a: Smear a thin streak of the same size of each liquid on the same plate in the same place at the same time. Time how long each takes to look dry. Only the liquid changes. The plate, the size of the streak, the warmth and the air stay the same.
items.why: A strong plan changes one thing, the liquid, and keeps the plate, the size of the streak, the place and the time the same.

items.p: A fridge cools its inside. What does it do with the heat it takes out?
opts: It gives it out to the room, mostly at the back
It destroys it
It stores it in the door
items.why: Heat is never destroyed. A fridge moves heat from inside to the pipes at the back, where it is given out to the room.

items.p: Label the drawing of a flat-bottomed cloud: warm air rising, air cooling, the height where the dew point is reached, the cloud base, the cloud.
items.a: Warm air rising from the ground. The air cooling as it climbs. A level line where it reaches its dew point. The cloud base at that line. The cloud above it.
items.why: A cloud begins where rising air has cooled to its dew point. All rising air cools to its dew point at about the same height, so the base is flat.
items.art: A hot field with an arrow of rising air going up to a small white cloud with a flat bottom, and five blank label lines.

items.p: Which one does not involve a solid turning straight into a gas?
opts: A camphor tablet shrinking in the open
An ice cube shrinking in a freezer
A puddle drying on the road
Frozen food drying out in a freezer
items.why: A puddle is liquid water, which evaporates. The other three are solids turning straight into gas.

items.p: Why is the dew point more useful than the humidity for knowing whether a glass will mist?
opts: The dew point is a temperature, so you can compare it with the temperature of the glass
The dew point never changes
The humidity is always wrong
items.why: Any surface colder than the dew point gets mist. Since the dew point is a temperature, it can be compared with the glass at once. Humidity is a percentage and needs the air temperature too.

items.p: Why do cooks drop a few grains of dry rice into a box of salt in the rainy season?
items.a: The rice takes up some of the water that gets into the box, so the salt stays loose and does not clump.
items.why: A strong answer says rice soaks up the moisture before the salt does, keeping the salt dry enough to pour.

items.p: Draw how the Sun's heat travels from the sea to a monsoon cloud and out again. Show the vapour, the cloud and the heat.
items.a: Sea water evaporating, with arrows of vapour carrying heat upward, a cloud forming where the vapour condenses, and heat arrows going out into the air around the cloud.
items.why: A good drawing shows heat being picked up by water as it evaporates and put down again as the vapour condenses.
items.art: An empty sea and sky with the Sun on the left.

items.p: The special liquid that moves heat in a fridge is called the ____.
items.why: The refrigerant evaporates inside the fridge, taking heat in, and condenses at the back, giving heat out.

items.p: Put these in order, from the one that dries fastest to the one that dries slowest.
items.why: Sanitiser dries in seconds, water in minutes, sugar syrup slowly and stickily, and coconut oil hardly at all.

items.p: The air temperature is 33 degrees and the dew point is 23 degrees. Using the rule of 125 metres for each degree of difference, about how high are the bottoms of the clouds, in metres?
items.why: 33 take away 23 is 10 degrees. 10 times 125 is 1250 metres.

items.p: In the Lid On or Lid Off test, the open pan lost 90 of its 500 millilitres and the covered pan lost 10 millilitres. Write a claim, the evidence and the reasoning.
items.a: Claim: a lid keeps almost all the water in a boiling pan. Evidence: the open pan lost 90 millilitres and the covered pan only 10. Reasoning: the vapour meets the cooler lid, turns back into drops and falls back into the pan.
items.why: A strong answer states the claim, uses both numbers as evidence and explains how the lid works.

items.p: Steam at 100 degrees burns skin worse than boiling water at 100 degrees. Why?
opts: Steam gives out a large amount of heat as it condenses on the skin, as well as the heat it gives out as it cools
Steam is hotter than 100 degrees
Water cannot burn
items.why: Steam carries a lot of latent heat, and gives it all up as it turns back into water on the skin. Boiling water gives up only the heat of cooling.

items.p: A room is 4 metres long, 3 metres wide and 3 metres high. The air in it is at 30 degrees and 60 per cent humidity, and a cubic metre of saturated air at 30 degrees holds 30 grams of vapour. About how many grams of water vapour are in the room?
items.why: The volume is 4 times 3 times 3, which is 36 cubic metres. 60 per cent of 30 grams is 18 grams in each cubic metre. 36 times 18 is 648 grams.

items.p: A school is choosing how to keep a hall cool in summer. Three people give advice.

views.says: Hang wet mats of khus grass on the windows and let the wind blow through. The water evaporating cools the air.
Wet mats will not help much here. The air is already nearly full of water, so little can evaporate. Use shade, fans and cross-breezes.
Buy an air conditioner. It works in any weather.

items.ask: Which advice would you follow for a school in dry Jodhpur, and which for a school in humid Kochi? Give a reason from what you know about evaporation. Then say one good point about another idea.
items.a: A strong answer says that wet mats cool well in dry air, because the water evaporates quickly and takes heat, but in humid air the water cannot evaporate much, so they help little. An air conditioner works in both but uses electricity and gives out heat outside. Fans and shade work anywhere, at low cost. A fair answer picks a different best choice for each place.
items.why: The best choice depends on how much water the air can still take. Evaporative cooling needs dry air, an air conditioner needs electricity, and fans and shade help everywhere.

items.p: A fridge door is left open all day in a closed kitchen. What happens to the temperature of the kitchen?
opts: It rises, because the fridge gives out heat at the back and the cold inside cannot cool the whole room
It falls, because the fridge is cold
It stays the same
items.why: A fridge moves heat from inside to the room, and its motor adds more. With the door open, it cannot cool the room, so the room warms a little.

items.p: Explain how a covered pan saves fuel as well as water.
items.a: The lid keeps the hot vapour in the pan. The vapour condenses on the lid and gives its heat back, and the drops fall back into the pan. So less heat escapes, and the water comes to the boil sooner and stays hot with less flame.
items.why: A strong answer says the lid keeps in the vapour and the heat it carries, and the condensing drops give the heat back to the pan.

items.p: Match each word to what it describes.
pairs: takes heat from what is left behind
gives heat out to what is around
a solid turning straight into a gas
the lowest temperature that evaporation can cool something to
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each word names a way that water or a solid changes state, and what happens to heat when it does.

items.p: At 30 degrees Celsius, air can carry about three times as much water vapour as air at 10 degrees.
items.why: True. At 10 degrees it is about 9 grams in each cubic metre, and at 30 degrees it is about 30 grams, a little more than three times as much.

items.p: Which one does not help sweat cool a person?
opts: A fan blowing on the skin
Dry air
Shade
Very humid air
items.why: Sweat cools only when it evaporates. In very humid air, sweat evaporates slowly, so it cools the body little. A fan, dry air and shade all help.

items.p: Why do the heaviest rains get heavier when the world warms?
items.a: Warmer air can carry more water vapour, about 7 per cent more for each degree. When that air rises and cools in a cloud, more water condenses and falls at once.
items.why: A strong answer joins the idea that warm air carries more vapour to the idea that rain falls when vapour condenses.

items.p: Draw a pressure cooker on a stove. Show where the pressure is high, and say why the water inside gets hotter than 100 degrees.
items.a: A closed pot with steam trapped inside, arrows showing pressure pushing on the lid and walls, and a label saying that the high pressure raises the boiling point.
items.why: The lid holds the steam in, so the pressure rises. At higher pressure, water boils at a higher temperature, and the hotter water cooks food faster.
items.art: An empty outline of a pressure cooker on a stove.

items.p: Will each glass get mist? Sort them.
items: a glass at 15 degrees, with a dew point of 20
a glass at 26 degrees, with a dew point of 20
a glass at 8 degrees, with a dew point of 12
a glass at 30 degrees, with a dew point of 28
items.a: see items
items.why: Any glass colder than the dew point gets mist. A glass warmer than the dew point stays dry.

items.p: A thermometer wrapped in a wet cloth reads lower than a dry one in the same air. In which air is the difference biggest?
opts: Dry air, because water evaporates fastest and takes the most heat
Very humid air
Air at exactly 100 per cent humidity
items.why: In dry air, the wet cloth's water evaporates quickly and takes much heat. In saturated air, water cannot evaporate, so the two thermometers read the same.

items.p: Label the humid box in the Thirsty Things test: the saucers of salt and other things, the bowl of hot water, the vapour, the lid, and the control jar outside.
items.a: The saucers inside the box. The bowl of hot water on the floor of the box. Vapour rising from the bowl. The lid closing the box. The jar of control salt outside.
items.why: The hot water fills the closed box with vapour. The things inside pull water from the air, and the control jar shows what dry air does.
items.art: A big plastic box with a lid, saucers and a bowl inside, a jar outside, and five blank label lines.

items.p: Put the steps of how a fridge works in order.
items: The vapour condenses at the back and gives out heat
The compressor squeezes the vapour and heats it
The liquid evaporates inside the fridge and takes in heat
a: The liquid evaporates inside the fridge and takes in heat
The compressor squeezes the vapour and heats it
The vapour condenses at the back and gives out heat
items.why: The refrigerant goes round a loop. It takes in heat inside as it evaporates, is squeezed, gives out heat outside as it condenses, and flows back.

items.p: A friend says ice cubes shrink in the freezer because they melt a little. How would you show that this is not the right explanation?
items.a: The freezer is below zero, so ice cannot melt there. You could weigh two cubes, leave one open in the freezer and seal the other in a box, and weigh them again after a few days. The open cube gets lighter and the walls get frost, so the ice has turned into vapour. The sealed one stays the same.
items.why: A strong answer uses a test with a sealed control, and points to the frost on the walls as the vapour landing again.

quiz.p: Hand sanitiser, water and coconut oil sit in the same air. Which will be gone first?
opts: Hand sanitiser, because its particles hold each other weakly
Coconut oil, because it is thinnest
Water, because it is clear
quiz.why: How fast a liquid leaves depends on how tightly its particles hold each other. Alcohol particles hold weakly, so they escape easily. Oil particles hold very tightly.

quiz.p: Why does wet skin feel cold when the water on it evaporates?
opts: The escaping water carries heat away from the skin
The water was cold to begin with
Evaporation makes new cold
quiz.why: The fastest, most energetic particles leave first and take their heat with them. The skin loses heat and feels cold.

quiz.p: What happens to heat when water vapour condenses into drops?
opts: The heat is given out to what is around
The heat is taken in
The heat disappears
quiz.why: Condensation gives out the same heat that evaporation took in. This is why steam burns badly and why the back of a fridge is warm.

quiz.p: Why is the back of a running fridge warm?
opts: It gives out heat taken from the inside
The food inside is hot
The door is open
quiz.why: A fridge moves heat from inside to the pipes at the back, where the refrigerant condenses and gives the heat out to the room.

quiz.p: Does a lid make the water in a pan boil at a higher temperature?
opts: No, a lid only keeps the vapour and heat in
Yes, a lid always makes water hotter than 100 degrees
Yes, if the lid is heavy
quiz.why: In an open or lidded pan, water boils at 100 degrees at sea level. The lid saves water and fuel. Only a pressure cooker, which holds in pressure, makes the water hotter.

quiz.p: Why does a pressure cooker cook dal faster?
opts: The higher pressure raises the boiling point, so the water is hotter
It uses more flame
It removes the water
quiz.why: The sealed cooker lets the pressure rise. At higher pressure, water boils at a higher temperature, so the food is cooked by hotter water.

quiz.p: The dew point of the air is 26 degrees. A steel glass of water is at 20 degrees. What happens?
opts: Mist forms on the outside of the glass
The glass stays dry
The glass gets hot
quiz.why: The glass is colder than the dew point, so water vapour in the air condenses on it.

quiz.p: Which can carry more water vapour in each cubic metre?
opts: Air at 30 degrees
Air at 10 degrees
Both the same
quiz.why: The most that air can carry rises quickly with temperature. At 30 degrees it is about 30 grams in each cubic metre, and at 10 degrees about 9.

quiz.p: Salt in an open dish goes damp on a very humid day. Where does the water come from?
opts: The salt pulls it out of the damp air
The salt makes water from itself
Water leaks up from the table
quiz.why: Salt holds water strongly, and when the air is damp enough, water vapour lands on it and stays. It does not need to be cold.

quiz.p: A camphor tablet gets smaller in the open and leaves no puddle. What has happened?
opts: It has turned straight from solid into gas
It has melted into the shelf
It has turned into water
quiz.why: This is sublimation. The camphor's particles escape directly into the air, which is why you can smell it.

quiz.p: William Cullen froze water using a pump and a liquid that boiled away fast. What did this show?
opts: A liquid can make cold just by evaporating, with no cold thing added
Ether is colder than ice
Water freezes when it is pumped
quiz.why: No cold thing was brought near. The cold came from the liquid leaving, which took heat from the water around it.

quiz.p: Why are the bottoms of fair-weather clouds flat and at about the same height?
opts: Rising air reaches its dew point at about the same height everywhere
The wind cuts them flat
The Sun melts the bottoms
quiz.why: Rising air cools as it climbs, and its vapour condenses where it reaches the dew point. That height is almost the same across a wide area.

applications: Fridges and air conditioners move heat by evaporating and condensing a liquid.
Pressure cookers raise the boiling point of water, so food cooks faster and uses less fuel.
Covering a pan with a lid saves fuel and water, because the vapour condenses on the lid and drips back.
Desert coolers and wet khus mats cool dry summer air by evaporating water into it.
Clay pots such as the matka and the surahi keep water cool as water seeps through the clay and evaporates from the outside.
Humans sweat and some other animals pant, to lose heat by evaporation.
Meteorologists use the dew point to forecast fog and the height of cloud bottoms.
Airports in the north of India plan around winter fog, which forms when air cools to its dew point.
Silica gel sachets keep shoes, cameras and medicines dry by pulling water vapour out of the air.
Cooks add rice grains to salt boxes in the monsoon to keep the salt loose.
Weather stations use evaporation pans to measure how much water the Sun takes from the land, which helps farmers plan irrigation.
Camphor and moth balls protect clothes and cupboards because they turn slowly into a gas that fills the space.
Freeze-dried foods are made by freezing food and letting the ice turn straight into vapour.

open_questions.q: How will clouds change as the world warms?
open_questions.why_open: Clouds can cool the Earth by reflecting sunlight and warm it by trapping heat. Scientists do not yet know how the balance will change, and it is the biggest uncertainty in forecasts of future warming.

open_questions.q: How much humid heat can a healthy person survive for several hours?
open_questions.why_open: An early calculation suggested a wet-bulb temperature of 35 degrees. Later tests with volunteers suggest the limit may be lower. The answer is still being measured, and it differs between young and old people.

open_questions.q: How do the first tiny ice crystals form in a cloud at temperatures well below zero?
open_questions.why_open: Pure water can stay liquid far below zero degrees until it meets a speck that helps it freeze. Scientists are still finding out which specks do this best, and exactly how.

open_questions.q: Can we cool buildings and food without electricity at large scale, by evaporation and shade?
open_questions.why_open: Clay pots and wet mats work in dry air, but they do less in humid air. Engineers are still searching for passive cooling that works in every climate.

open_questions.q: Can sea spray be used to make low clouds brighter and cool a hot region?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists have suggested spraying tiny sea salt drops into low clouds, to make them reflect more sunlight. Others fear side effects. It has been tried only in tiny tests, and the effects are unknown.

open_questions.q: How exactly does a water molecule leave the surface of a liquid, moment by moment?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can calculate it with computers and observe it with fast lasers, but the details of how water molecules leave and return at a surface are still being measured and argued over.

maths.problem: In the Drop Race, the sanitiser streak looked dry after 1 minute, the vinegar after 6 minutes, the water after 9 minutes and the salt water after 11 minutes. How many minutes longer did the water take than the sanitiser? How many times as long?
maths.answer: 8 minutes longer, and 9 times as long.
maths.explain: 9 take away 1 is 8. 9 divided by 1 is 9, so the water took 9 times as long as the sanitiser.
maths.context: These are made-up results from the Drop Race, where six liquids dry on a plate.
maths.why_maths: Comparing times by taking away and by dividing shows both how much longer and how many times longer something took.

maths.problem: A cubic metre of air at 30 degrees Celsius can carry at most about 30 grams of water vapour. The air is at 50 per cent humidity. How many grams are in each cubic metre? How many grams are in a room that holds 36 cubic metres?
maths.answer: 15 grams in each cubic metre, and 540 grams in the room.
maths.explain: 50 per cent is a half. Half of 30 is 15. In 36 cubic metres there are 36 times 15, which is 540 grams.
maths.context: This is about how much water vapour there is in the air of a room.
maths.why_maths: Turning a percentage into a fraction of a known amount tells you how much water the air really carries.

maths.problem: A cubic metre of saturated air at 30 degrees holds 30 grams of vapour. When it is cooled to 20 degrees, it can hold only 17 grams. How many grams condense from each cubic metre? How many grams condense from a room of 36 cubic metres?
maths.answer: 13 grams from each cubic metre, and 468 grams from the room.
maths.explain: 30 take away 17 is 13 grams. 36 times 13 is 468 grams, which is nearly half a litre of water.
maths.context: This is about the water that forms when damp air cools.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting and then multiplying shows how large the amount of dew or fog can be, even from air that looks empty.

maths.problem: In the Lid On or Lid Off test, the open pan lost 90 millilitres of its 500 millilitres, and the covered pan lost 10 millilitres. How many times as much water did the open pan lose? What fraction of its water did the covered pan lose?
maths.answer: 9 times as much, and one fiftieth.
maths.explain: 90 divided by 10 is 9. The covered pan lost 10 out of 500, which is 1 out of 50.
maths.context: These are made-up results from the Lid On or Lid Off test.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the two losses and writing one as a fraction of the whole shows how much difference a lid makes.

maths.problem: In the Evaporation Pan project, the depth in the sunny jar was 60, 55, 50, 47, 41, 38 and 33 millimetres on seven days. How many millimetres did it lose in the six days between the first reading and the last? What is the average loss each day?
maths.answer: 27 millimetres in six days, and about 4 and a half millimetres each day.
maths.explain: 60 take away 33 is 27. 27 divided by 6 is 4 and a half.
maths.context: These are made-up readings from the Evaporation Pan project.
maths.why_maths: Finding the total change and sharing it over the days gives a typical loss for a day, which you can compare between jars.

maths.problem: The temperature is 34 degrees Celsius and the dew point is 22 degrees. For each degree of difference between them, the cloud bottoms are about 125 metres higher. How many metres up are the cloud bottoms? How many kilometres is that?
maths.answer: 1500 metres, which is 1 and a half kilometres.
maths.explain: 34 take away 22 is 12. 12 times 125 is 1500 metres. 1000 metres make a kilometre, so that is 1 and a half kilometres.
maths.context: This is about the Flat-Bottomed Clouds activity.
maths.why_maths: A short sum and a unit change turn two weather numbers into a height you can picture.

maths.problem: Water boils about 1 degree lower for every 300 metres you climb. Ooty is about 2,200 metres above sea level. About how many degrees lower does water boil at Ooty than at sea level? What temperature is that?
maths.answer: About 7 degrees lower, so about 93 degrees (about 92 or 93 is the usual figure for Ooty).
maths.explain: 2,200 divided by 300 is a little over 7. 100 take away 7 is 93.
maths.context: This is about how boiling depends on height.
maths.why_maths: Dividing a height by 300 tells you how far the boiling point falls, so you can predict it for any hill.

maths.problem: Warming 1 kilogram of water from 0 to 100 degrees takes about 420 units of heat. Boiling the same kilogram away takes about 2,260 units. About how many times as much is that? Round to the nearest whole number.
maths.explain: Round the numbers to make the sum easy. 2,260 is about 2,200 and 420 is about 440, and 2,200 divided by 440 is 5. So boiling away takes about 5 times as much heat.
maths.context: This is about why steam carries so much heat.
maths.why_maths: Estimating with round numbers shows quickly how much more heat it takes to turn water into vapour than to warm it.

maths.problem: In the Will It Mist? card game, 13 of the 24 air and glass cards say MIST. If you turn over one card without looking, is it more likely to say MIST or NO MIST? What fraction of the cards say MIST?
maths.answer: MIST is a little more likely, and 13 out of 24 cards say MIST.
maths.explain: 13 cards say MIST and 24 take away 13 is 11 that say NO MIST. 13 is more than 11, so MIST is a little more likely. The fraction is 13 out of 24.
maths.context: This is about the cards in the Will It Mist? game.
maths.why_maths: Counting the cards in each group tells you what is more likely to turn up, before you draw.

The Drop Race uses thin streaks, not drops, because a thin streak of water dries in minutes while a bead can take over an hour. Salt and jaggery should go damp in forty minutes, sugar a little tacky, and rice and baking soda should stay the same.
